\section{Introduction}

\subsection{A category error and its repair}
Category theory is often advertised as the universal language of mathematics, and
the topos is one of its most expressive sentences. A topos behaves like a
self-contained mathematical universe: it has finite limits, exponentials, and a
\emph{subobject classifier} $\Omega$, the object internalizing truth values. A
Grothendieck topos is, concretely, a category of sheaves on a site.

A bold version of the universality slogan asserts that \emph{every Grothendieck
topos is a bounded lattice with a universal property}. As literally stated this is
a \textbf{category error}. A bounded lattice is a partially ordered set; a topos
is a category in which there are generally many distinct morphisms between two
objects, so it is not a poset. The category of sets $\mathbf{Set}$ is the simplest
counterexample.

The repair is to relocate the lattice. Fix an object $X$ of a topos $E$. Its
\emph{subobjects} form a poset $\Sub(X)$, and this poset \emph{is} a bounded
lattice; in fact it is a \textbf{frame} (complete Heyting algebra). The universal
property survives intact: it is the adjunction between meet and Heyting
implication. We formalize and prove the surviving statement over an abstract frame
$\alpha$, and point to the explicit topological model $\Opens X$.

\subsection{Why one proof covers three subjects}
The frame axioms are exactly the algebraic content shared by: \textbf{topology}
(the open sets $\Opens X$ of a space $X$ form a frame under $\subseteq$, the
subobject lattice of the terminal sheaf on $X$); \textbf{logic} (the
Lindenbaum--Tarski algebra of intuitionistic propositional logic, with $\himp$
implication and $a^c = a \himp \bot$ negation); and \textbf{category theory}
($\Sub(X)$ in any topos, with $\Omega$ internalizing the structure). Because all
three are instances of a frame, a single theorem proved for abstract $\alpha$
discharges all three. This is the precise sense in which the development is a
\emph{bridge}.

\section{Preliminaries: frames and Heyting algebras}

Throughout, $\alpha$ is a \textbf{frame}: a complete lattice in which binary meet
distributes over arbitrary joins, $a \meet \bigsqcup_i b_i = \bigsqcup_i (a \meet
b_i)$. Every frame is a complete Heyting algebra: there is a binary operation
$\himp$ (Heyting implication) with the adjunction property
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adj}
  a \meet x \le c \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x \le (a \himp c).
\end{equation}

\begin{definition}[Pseudocomplement]
The \emph{pseudocomplement} of $a$ is $a^c := a \himp \bot$, the largest element
disjoint from $a$ (so $a \meet a^c = \bot$). The complement is order-reversing:
$a \le b$ implies $b^c \le a^c$.
\end{definition}

We use the standard frame/Heyting identities: $a \meet (a \himp c) \le c$;
\eqref{eq:adj}; $a \le a^{cc}$; antitonicity of $(\cdot)^c$; the
\textbf{triple-negation law} $a^{ccc} = a^c$; the distributive law
$(a \meet b)^{cc} = a^{cc} \meet b^{cc}$; and the boundary identities $\bot^c =
\top$, $\top^c = \bot$.

\paragraph{Background (Knaster--Tarski).}
For a complete lattice and $f : \alpha \to \alpha$, set
$\preFixed(f) = \{x : f x \le x\}$ and $\postFixed(f) = \{x : x \le f x\}$.

\begin{theorem}[Knaster--Tarski; Lean: \texttt{knaster\_tarski}]\label{thm:kt}
If $f$ is monotone then $f(\inf \preFixed(f)) = \inf \preFixed(f)$; the infimum of
the pre-fixed points is the least fixed point. Dually $f(\sup \postFixed(f))$ is
the greatest fixed point.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For every $b \in \preFixed(f)$, $\inf \le b$ gives $f(\inf) \le f(b) \le b$, so
$f(\inf) \le \inf$. Monotonicity gives $f(f(\inf)) \le f(\inf)$, so $f(\inf) \in
\preFixed(f)$, whence $\inf \le f(\inf)$. Antisymmetry concludes.
\end{proof}

\section{The universal property of the subobject lattice}

\begin{theorem}[Universal property; Lean: \texttt{himp\_isGreatest}]\label{thm:univ}
For all $a, c \in \alpha$,
\[
  a \himp c \;=\; \max\{\, x \in \alpha : a \meet x \le c \,\},
  \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \IsGreatest\,\{x \mid a \meet x \le c\}\,(a \himp c).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
\emph{Membership:} $a \meet (a \himp c) \le c$. \emph{Upper bound:} given $x$ with
$a \meet x \le c$, the adjunction \eqref{eq:adj} together with commutativity
$a \meet x = x \meet a$ gives $x \le a \himp c$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Theorem~\ref{thm:univ} says $(a \meet \cdot)$ is left adjoint to $(a \himp
\cdot)$: conjunction and implication form an adjoint pair. This adjunction is the
categorical-semantics content meant by ``bounded lattice with a universal
property.'' In topology $a \himp c$ is the largest open set whose intersection
with $a$ lands in $c$; in logic it is the deductively strongest $x$ with $a \meet
x \vdash c$.
\end{remark}

\section{Double negation is a nucleus}

\begin{definition}[Lean: \texttt{dneg}]
The \emph{double-negation operator} is $\dneg a := a^{cc}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nucleus laws]\label{thm:nucleus}
For all $a, b \in \alpha$:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \texttt{le\_dneg}: $a \le \dneg a$ \quad(extensive);
  \item \texttt{dneg\_monotone}: $a \le b \Rightarrow \dneg a \le \dneg b$ \quad(monotone);
  \item \texttt{dneg\_idem}: $\dneg(\dneg a) = \dneg a$ \quad(idempotent);
  \item \texttt{dneg\_inf}: $\dneg(a \meet b) = \dneg a \meet \dneg b$ \quad(meet-preserving);
  \item \texttt{dneg\_bot}/\texttt{dneg\_top}: $\dneg \bot = \bot$ and $\dneg \top = \top$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(1) $a \le a^{cc}$.
(2) $(\cdot)^c$ is order-reversing, so applied twice it is order-preserving: from
$a \le b$ get $b^c \le a^c$ then $a^{cc} \le b^{cc}$.
(3) $\dneg(\dneg a) = a^{cccc}$; by the triple-negation law $a^{ccc} = a^c$,
$a^{cccc} = (a^{ccc})^c = (a^c)^c = a^{cc} = \dneg a$.
(4) $(a \meet b)^{cc} = a^{cc} \meet b^{cc}$ is the distributive law.
(5) $\bot^{cc} = \top^c = \bot$; $\top^{cc} = \bot^c = \top$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Properties (1)--(4) are exactly the axioms of a \textbf{nucleus} (=
Lawvere--Tierney topology, internalized): a meet-preserving closure operator. The
nucleus $\dneg$ yields the \textbf{double-negation subtopos}, the smallest dense
subtopos, whose internal logic is Boolean. On $\Opens X$, $\dneg$ is
``interior of the closure.'' Crucially $\dneg$ is \emph{not} join-preserving and
$a^{cc} = a$ fails intuitionistically; no proof above uses classical
$a^{cc} = a$.
\end{remark}

\section{Regular elements}

\begin{definition}[Lean: \texttt{IsRegular}]
An element $a$ is \emph{regular} if $\dneg a = a$. The regular elements are the
fixed points of the nucleus.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Lean: \texttt{isRegular\_bot}, \texttt{isRegular\_top}]\label{cor:reg-bounds}
$\bot$ and $\top$ are regular.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:nucleus}(5).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Meet-closure; Lean: \texttt{isRegular\_inf}]\label{thm:reg-inf}
If $a$ and $b$ are regular then $a \meet b$ is regular.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\dneg(a \meet b) = \dneg a \meet \dneg b = a \meet b$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:nucleus}(4) and the hypotheses.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[One-sided recognition; Lean: \texttt{isRegular\_iff}]\label{lem:reg-iff}
$a$ is regular iff $\dneg a \le a$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $\dneg a = a$ then $\dneg a \le a$. Conversely, from $\dneg a \le a$ and the
always-true $a \le \dneg a$, antisymmetry gives $\dneg a = a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Corollary~\ref{cor:reg-bounds} and Theorem~\ref{thm:reg-inf} show the regular
elements form a bounded sub-meet-lattice --- the objects of the double-negation
sheaf subtopos. Classically this sublattice is a Boolean algebra with join
$a \join' b := (a^c \meet b^c)^c$ and complement $a^c$; the present results
establish the bounded and meet-closed parts. Lemma~\ref{lem:reg-iff} is the
practical recognition tool.
\end{remark}

\section{Fixed points via Knaster--Tarski}

Since $\dneg$ is monotone (Theorem~\ref{thm:nucleus}(2)) it falls within the
framework of Theorem~\ref{thm:kt}.

\begin{theorem}[Extremal fixed points]\label{thm:fp}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \texttt{lfp\_dneg\_eq\_bot}: $\inf \preFixed(\dneg) = \bot$.
  \item \texttt{gfp\_dneg\_eq\_top}: $\sup \postFixed(\dneg) = \top$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(1) $\bot \in \preFixed(\dneg)$ since $\dneg \bot = \bot \le \bot$, so
$\inf \preFixed(\dneg) \le \bot$; the reverse is $\bot \le \cdot$.
(2) $\sup \postFixed(\dneg) \le \top$ trivially; and $\top \le \sup$ because
$\top \in \postFixed(\dneg)$, i.e. $\top \le \dneg \top$ by extensivity. (Indeed
every $a$ is post-fixed, since $a \le \dneg a$.)
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Lean: \texttt{dneg\_knaster\_tarski}]
The infimum of pre-fixed points of $\dneg$ is a genuine fixed point:
$\dneg(\inf \preFixed(\dneg)) = \inf \preFixed(\dneg)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:kt} to the monotone $\dneg$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:fp}(1) the
fixed point is $\bot$.
\end{proof}

\section{The topological witness}

All results instantiate at $\alpha = \Opens X$, the frame of open sets of a space
$X$, the subobject lattice of the terminal object of the sheaf topos $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$:
$\meet = \cap$, $\join = \bigcup$, $\top = X$, $\bot = \emptyset$;
$a \himp c = \operatorname{int}((X \setminus a) \cup c)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:univ});
$a^c = \operatorname{int}(X \setminus a)$, the exterior of $a$;
$\dneg a = \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{cl}(a))$, the regularization
(Theorem~\ref{thm:nucleus}); regular elements are the \emph{regular open sets},
closed under $\cap$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:reg-inf}); and the extremal regularization
fixed points are $\emptyset$ and $X$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:fp}). Thus the abstract
bridge becomes concrete: \emph{double negation $=$ interior of closure}, and
\emph{regular elements $=$ regular open sets}.

\section{A worked example: a four-element diamond frame}

Fix the poset $P$ on four points $\{0,1,2,3\}$ with $0 < 1 < 3$, $0 < 2 < 3$ (a
diamond). Take $\alpha$ to be the lattice of down-sets of $P$ --- the
Alexandrov-open sets of the finite space $P$. There are exactly six:
\[
\bot = \emptyset,\; \{0\},\; \{0,1\},\; \{0,2\},\; \{0,1,2\},\;
\{0,1,2,3\} = \top .
\]
Meet is intersection, join union, and $a^c = \bigcup\{x : a \cap x = \emptyset\}$.
Every nonempty down-set contains the minimum $0$, so the only down-set disjoint
from a nonempty $a$ is $\emptyset$; hence $a^c = \bot$ for $a \ne \bot$ and
$\bot^c = \top$, giving
\[
\dneg \bot = \bot, \qquad \dneg a = \top \text{ for every } a \ne \bot .
\]
Every theorem can be read off this table. Extensivity, idempotence and
meet-preservation (Theorem~\ref{thm:nucleus}) hold by inspection; the fixed
points of $\dneg$ are exactly $\{\bot, \top\}$, so the regular elements form the
two-element Boolean algebra (Definition, Theorem~\ref{thm:reg-inf}). The
pre-fixed points are $\{\bot,\top\}$ with infimum $\bot$, while \emph{every}
element is post-fixed, with supremum $\top$, confirming Theorem~\ref{thm:fp}. For
the universal property, with $a = \{0,1,2\}$ and $c = \{0,1\}$ the down-sets $x$
with $a \cap x \subseteq c$ are $\emptyset, \{0\}, \{0,1\}$, whose join $\{0,1\}$
is the greatest witness $a \himp c$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:univ}). On an antichain
(a discrete space) every element is regular and the frame is already Boolean; the
diamond shows the generic intuitionistic behaviour --- a rich lattice with a tiny
classical core.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{The corrected grand claim}
The honest theorem behind ``every Grothendieck topos is a bounded lattice with a
universal property'' is: \emph{in any topos, the subobjects of a fixed object form
a frame; meet has a right adjoint (Heyting implication, Theorem~\ref{thm:univ}),
and double negation is a nucleus (Theorem~\ref{thm:nucleus}). The universal
property is the meet--implication adjunction.} The failure of the literal slogan
is a category error (``topos'' vs.\ ``its subobject lattice'').

\subsection{Historical and structural context}
The frame/locale viewpoint (``topology without points'') and the theory of
locales provide the topological side; Heyting algebras are the algebraic
semantics of intuitionistic logic; nuclei correspond to sublocales, and
Lawvere--Tierney topologies to subtoposes. The nucleus $a^{cc}$ defines the
double-negation subtopos, the smallest dense subtopos, which is always Boolean.
The fixed-point side is Knaster--Tarski. The present contribution is a compact,
uniform, fully verified account over a single abstract frame, isolating the
meet--implication adjunction as the honest universal property and computing the
extremal fixed points explicitly.

\subsection{Relation to the double-negation translation}
The Gödel--Gentzen double-negation translation embeds classical logic into
intuitionistic logic; its semantic shadow is the nucleus $\dneg$, and passing to
$\dneg$-fixed points collapses the intuitionistic frame to its Boolean core. The
four nucleus laws are the algebraic backbone of that translation.

\subsection{Limitations}
We prove the bounded and meet-closed structure of regular elements, not the full
Boolean algebra, and treat the abstract frame rather than the $2$-categorical
topos itself.

\section{Future directions}

\paragraph{FD-1 (Regular subobjects form a Boolean algebra).}
For every frame, the fixed points of $\dneg$ carry a Boolean algebra structure
with meet $\meet$, bounds $\top/\bot$, complement $a^c$, and join $a \join' b :=
(a^c \meet b^c)^c$. Meet-preservation plus idempotence force Booleanness on the
fixed points. Closure under $\meet$ and the bounds are already established; only de
Morgan join/complement laws remain.

\paragraph{FD-2 (Yoneda iso-corollary upgrades to an equivalence of groupoids).}
$X \mapsto \mathrm{yoneda}(X)$ induces an equivalence between the core groupoid of
$C$ and the full subcategory of representable presheaves; the object-level
biconditional \texttt{iso\_iff\_representable\_iso} is its $\pi_0$ shadow.

\paragraph{FD-3 ($\dneg$ is the unique nontrivial topology on a chain).}
On a totally ordered frame, every nucleus other than the identity equals $\dneg$
collapsed onto $\{\bot, \top\}$; chains admit only the trivial and the
double-negation topologies.

\paragraph{FD-4 (Knaster--Tarski computes sheafification of any nucleus).}
For an arbitrary nucleus $j$, $\inf\{x : a \le x \wedge j x \le x\} = j a$,
exhibiting sheafification as the Knaster--Tarski least-fixed-point closure
relative to $a$.

\section{Conclusion}

Starting from a slogan that is literally false, we isolated and proved its true
core: the subobject lattice of a topos is a frame whose meet--implication
adjunction is a genuine universal property; double negation on it is a nucleus;
the regular elements form a bounded, meet-closed sublattice (the classical core);
and the nucleus's extremal fixed points are $\bot$ and $\top$, recovered through
Knaster--Tarski. Each statement is simultaneously topological, logical, and
categorical, with the frame --- witnessed concretely by $\Opens X$ --- the place
where the three meet.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Callable, FrozenSet, List, Set, Tuple

# A frame element is a down-closed set of poset points, stored as a frozenset.
Elt = FrozenSet[int]


class Frame:
    """The frame of down-sets of a finite poset (a complete Heyting algebra)."""

    def __init__(self, points: List[int], leq: Callable[[int, int], bool]) -> None:
        self.points: List[int] = points
        self.leq = leq  # leq(p, q) means p ≤ q in the poset
        self.elements: List[Elt] = self._all_downsets()
        self.bot: Elt = frozenset()
        self.top: Elt = frozenset(points)

    def _is_downset(self, s: Set[int]) -> bool:
        # s is down-closed: q ∈ s and p ≤ q ⟹ p ∈ s
        return all(p in s for q in s for p in self.points if self.leq(p, q))

    def _all_downsets(self) -> List[Elt]:
        downs: List[Elt] = []
        n = len(self.points)
        for r in range(n + 1):
            for combo in combinations(self.points, r):
                s = set(combo)
                if self._is_downset(s):
                    downs.append(frozenset(s))
        return downs

    # ---- lattice operations ------------------------------------------------
    def meet(self, a: Elt, b: Elt) -> Elt:
        return a & b

    def join(self, a: Elt, b: Elt) -> Elt:
        return a | b

    def le(self, a: Elt, b: Elt) -> bool:
        return a <= b

    def himp(self, a: Elt, c: Elt) -> Elt:
        """Heyting implication: the join of every element x with a ⊓ x ≤ c.

        In a frame this join itself satisfies the constraint, so it is the
        *greatest* such x (this is exactly `himp_isGreatest`).
        """
        result: Set[int] = set()
        for x in self.elements:
            if self.le(self.meet(a, x), c):
                result |= x
        return frozenset(result)

    def compl(self, a: Elt) -> Elt:
        """Pseudocomplement aᶜ = a ⇨ ⊥."""
        return self.himp(a, self.bot)

    def dneg(self, a: Elt) -> Elt:
        """Double negation aᶜᶜ — the nucleus / regularization operator."""
        return self.compl(self.compl(a))

    def is_regular(self, a: Elt) -> bool:
        return self.dneg(a) == a


def fmt(a: Elt) -> str:
    return "{" + ",".join(map(str, sorted(a))) + "}" if a else "∅"


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theorem checkers (each returns True iff the theorem holds on this frame).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check_himp_isGreatest(F: Frame) -> bool:
    for a in F.elements:
        for c in F.elements:
            h = F.himp(a, c)
            witnesses = [x for x in F.elements if F.le(F.meet(a, x), c)]
            # membership: a ⊓ h ≤ c
            if not F.le(F.meet(a, h), c):
                return False
            # greatest: every witness is below h
            if not all(F.le(x, h) for x in witnesses):
                return False
    return True


def check_le_dneg(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(F.le(a, F.dneg(a)) for a in F.elements)


def check_dneg_monotone(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(
        (not F.le(a, b)) or F.le(F.dneg(a), F.dneg(b))
        for a in F.elements
        for b in F.elements
    )


def check_dneg_idem(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(F.dneg(F.dneg(a)) == F.dneg(a) for a in F.elements)


def check_dneg_inf(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(
        F.dneg(F.meet(a, b)) == F.meet(F.dneg(a), F.dneg(b))
        for a in F.elements
        for b in F.elements
    )


def check_dneg_bounds(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return F.dneg(F.bot) == F.bot and F.dneg(F.top) == F.top


def check_isRegular_inf(F: Frame) -> bool:
    for a in F.elements:
        for b in F.elements:
            if F.is_regular(a) and F.is_regular(b):
                if not F.is_regular(F.meet(a, b)):
                    return False
    return True


def check_isRegular_iff(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(
        F.is_regular(a) == F.le(F.dneg(a), a) for a in F.elements
    )


def lfp_dneg(F: Frame) -> Elt:
    """sInf of pre-fixed points {x | dneg x ≤ x} = intersection of them."""
    pre = [x for x in F.elements if F.le(F.dneg(x), x)]
    acc = F.top
    for x in pre:
        acc = F.meet(acc, x)
    return acc


def gfp_dneg(F: Frame) -> Elt:
    """sSup of post-fixed points {x | x ≤ dneg x} = union of them."""
    post = [x for x in F.elements if F.le(x, F.dneg(x))]
    acc = F.bot
    for x in post:
        acc = F.join(acc, x)
    return acc


def run_on(name: str, F: Frame) -> Tuple[str, bool]:
    print(f"\n=== Frame: {name} ===")
    print(f"  elements ({len(F.elements)}): " + ", ".join(fmt(a) for a in F.elements))
    regs = [a for a in F.elements if F.is_regular(a)]
    print(f"  regular elements: " + ", ".join(fmt(a) for a in regs))
    print(f"  example: dneg{fmt(F.elements[1])} = {fmt(F.dneg(F.elements[1]))}")

    checks = {
        "himp_isGreatest": check_himp_isGreatest(F),
        "le_dneg": check_le_dneg(F),
        "dneg_monotone": check_dneg_monotone(F),
        "dneg_idem": check_dneg_idem(F),
        "dneg_inf": check_dneg_inf(F),
        "dneg_bot/dneg_top": check_dneg_bounds(F),
        "isRegular_inf": check_isRegular_inf(F),
        "isRegular_iff": check_isRegular_iff(F),
        "lfp_dneg_eq_bot": lfp_dneg(F) == F.bot,
        "gfp_dneg_eq_top": gfp_dneg(F) == F.top,
    }
    for k, v in checks.items():
        print(f"    [{'PASS' if v else 'FAIL'}] {k}")
    print(f"  lfp(dneg) = {fmt(lfp_dneg(F))}   gfp(dneg) = {fmt(gfp_dneg(F))}")
    return name, all(checks.values())


def main() -> None:
    # (1) Two-element chain 0 < 1: down-sets ∅ ⊂ {0} ⊂ {0,1}.
    #     {0} is NOT regular: dneg{0} = ⊤. This is the intuitionistic phenomenon.
    chain = Frame([0, 1], lambda p, q: p == q or (p == 0 and q == 1))

    # (2) Three-element chain 0 < 1 < 2 (a longer Heyting chain).
    def chain3_leq(p: int, q: int) -> bool:
        return p <= q
    chain3 = Frame([0, 1, 2], chain3_leq)

    # (3) "V" poset: 0 < 2, 1 < 2 (two minimal points under a top).
    def v_leq(p: int, q: int) -> bool:
        if p == q:
            return True
        return q == 2 and p in (0, 1)
    vshape = Frame([0, 1, 2], v_leq)

    # (4) Diamond poset 0 < 1, 0 < 2, 1 < 3, 2 < 3.
    diamond_edges = {(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (0, 3)}

    def diamond_leq(p: int, q: int) -> bool:
        return p == q or (p, q) in diamond_edges
    diamond = Frame([0, 1, 2, 3], diamond_leq)

    results = [
        run_on("2-chain (0<1)", chain),
        run_on("3-chain (0<1<2)", chain3),
        run_on("V-poset (0<2, 1<2)", vshape),
        run_on("diamond (0<1,2<3)", diamond),
    ]

    print("\n" + "=" * 48)
    ok = all(r[1] for r in results)
    for name, passed in results:
        print(f"  {'ALL PASS' if passed else 'SOME FAIL'} :: {name}")
    print(f"\nOverall: {'ALL THEOREMS VERIFIED' if ok else 'FAILURE DETECTED'}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import Mathlib
import Bridges.KnasterTarskiBridge

/-! # The Subobject Lattice of a Topos: Double Negation as a Nucleus

In any (Grothendieck) topos, the subobjects of a fixed object form a complete
Heyting algebra (a frame): a bounded, distributive lattice whose meet `⊓` has a
right adjoint `⇨` (Heyting implication) — and that adjunction *is* the universal
property.  We model the subobject lattice abstractly by `Order.Frame α`.

* `himp_isGreatest` — the universal property: `a ⇨ c` is the greatest `x` with
  `a ⊓ x ≤ c`.
* `dneg` (double negation `a ↦ aᶜᶜ`) is a nucleus / closure operator: extensive
  (`le_dneg`), monotone (`dneg_monotone`), idempotent (`dneg_idem`), and
  meet-preserving (`dneg_inf`).
* `dneg_bot`, `dneg_top` — the bounds are regular.
* `IsRegular` elements are closed under `⊓` (`isRegular_inf`).
* The least fixed point of the nucleus is `⊥` (`lfp_dneg_eq_bot`) and the
  greatest is `⊤` (`gfp_dneg_eq_top`).
-/

open CategoryTheory KnasterTarskiBridge

namespace ToposDoubleNegationLattice

universe u

variable {α : Type u} [Order.Frame α]

/-! ## Section 1 — The universal property of the subobject lattice -/

/-- **Universal property of the topos subobject lattice.** Heyting implication
`a ⇨ c` is the *greatest* element `x` whose meet with `a` lands below `c`. -/
theorem himp_isGreatest (a c : α) : IsGreatest {x | a ⊓ x ≤ c} (a ⇨ c) := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · show a ⊓ (a ⇨ c) ≤ c
    exact inf_himp_le
  · intro x hx
    rw [le_himp_iff, inf_comm]
    exact hx

/-! ## Section 2 — Double negation is a nucleus (closure operator) -/

/-- The double-negation operator `a ↦ aᶜᶜ` on the subobject lattice. -/
def dneg (a : α) : α := aᶜᶜ

/-- **Extensive.** Every element is below its double negation: `a ≤ aᶜᶜ`. -/
theorem le_dneg (a : α) : a ≤ dneg a := le_compl_compl

/-- **Monotone.** Double negation is order preserving. -/
theorem dneg_monotone : Monotone (dneg : α → α) := by
  intro a b h
  exact compl_le_compl (compl_le_compl h)

/-- **Idempotent.** `aᶜᶜᶜᶜ = aᶜᶜ`, via the triple-negation law `aᶜᶜᶜ = aᶜ`. -/
theorem dneg_idem (a : α) : dneg (dneg a) = dneg a := by
  show aᶜᶜᶜᶜ = aᶜᶜ
  rw [compl_compl_compl]

/-- **Meet-preserving.** `(a ⊓ b)ᶜᶜ = aᶜᶜ ⊓ bᶜᶜ`. -/
theorem dneg_inf (a b : α) : dneg (a ⊓ b) = dneg a ⊓ dneg b :=
  compl_compl_inf_distrib a b

/-- The bottom subobject is regular: `⊥ᶜᶜ = ⊥`. -/
@[simp] theorem dneg_bot : dneg (⊥ : α) = ⊥ := by
  show (⊥ : α)ᶜᶜ = ⊥
  rw [compl_bot, compl_top]

/-- The top subobject (the whole object) is regular: `⊤ᶜᶜ = ⊤`. -/
@[simp] theorem dneg_top : dneg (⊤ : α) = ⊤ := by
  show (⊤ : α)ᶜᶜ = ⊤
  rw [compl_top, compl_bot]

/-! ## Section 3 — Regular elements form a bounded sub-meet-lattice -/

/-- A subobject is **regular** when it is a fixed point of double negation. -/
def IsRegular (a : α) : Prop := dneg a = a

theorem isRegular_bot : IsRegular (⊥ : α) := dneg_bot
theorem isRegular_top : IsRegular (⊤ : α) := dneg_top

/-- Regular elements are closed under meet. -/
theorem isRegular_inf {a b : α} (ha : IsRegular a) (hb : IsRegular b) :
    IsRegular (a ⊓ b) := by
  unfold IsRegular at *
  rw [dneg_inf, ha, hb]

/-- An element is regular iff it is "stable": `aᶜᶜ ≤ a`. -/
theorem isRegular_iff (a : α) : IsRegular a ↔ dneg a ≤ a := by
  constructor
  · intro h; rw [h]
  · intro h; exact le_antisymm h (le_dneg a)

/-! ## Section 4 — Catalog bridge: the nucleus inside Knaster–Tarski -/

/-- The Knaster–Tarski least fixed point of the double-negation nucleus is `⊥`. -/
theorem lfp_dneg_eq_bot : sInf (preFixed (dneg : α → α)) = ⊥ := by
  apply le_antisymm
  · apply sInf_le
    show dneg (⊥ : α) ≤ ⊥
    rw [dneg_bot]
  · exact bot_le

/-- The Knaster–Tarski greatest fixed point of the double-negation nucleus is `⊤`. -/
theorem gfp_dneg_eq_top : sSup (postFixed (dneg : α → α)) = ⊤ := by
  apply le_antisymm
  · exact le_top
  · apply le_sSup
    exact le_dneg ⊤

/-- `dneg`'s `sInf`-of-pre-fixed-points is genuinely a fixed point. -/
theorem dneg_knaster_tarski :
    dneg (sInf (preFixed (dneg : α → α))) = sInf (preFixed (dneg : α → α)) :=
  knaster_tarski dneg dneg_monotone

/-! ## Section 5 — The topological witness: the frame of opens

Everything above instantiates at `TopologicalSpace.Opens X`, the subobject
lattice of the terminal object in the sheaf topos `Sh(X)`: there `dneg` is the
regularization `interior ∘ closure`, and the regular elements are exactly the
regular open sets. -/

end ToposDoubleNegationLattice

Down-sets of any poset form a complete Heyting algebra — the Alexandrov-open
sets of a finite topological space — so it is a faithful finite model of the
subobject lattice `Opens X`.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Callable, FrozenSet, List, Set, Tuple

# A frame element is a down-closed set of poset points, stored as a frozenset.
Elt = FrozenSet[int]


class Frame:
    """The frame of down-sets of a finite poset (a complete Heyting algebra)."""

    def __init__(self, points: List[int], leq: Callable[[int, int], bool]) -> None:
        self.points: List[int] = points
        self.leq = leq  # leq(p, q) means p ≤ q in the poset
        self.elements: List[Elt] = self._all_downsets()
        self.bot: Elt = frozenset()
        self.top: Elt = frozenset(points)

    def _is_downset(self, s: Set[int]) -> bool:
        # s is down-closed: q ∈ s and p ≤ q ⟹ p ∈ s
        return all(p in s for q in s for p in self.points if self.leq(p, q))

    def _all_downsets(self) -> List[Elt]:
        downs: List[Elt] = []
        n = len(self.points)
        for r in range(n + 1):
            for combo in combinations(self.points, r):
                s = set(combo)
                if self._is_downset(s):
                    downs.append(frozenset(s))
        return downs

    # ---- lattice operations ------------------------------------------------
    def meet(self, a: Elt, b: Elt) -> Elt:
        return a & b

    def join(self, a: Elt, b: Elt) -> Elt:
        return a | b

    def le(self, a: Elt, b: Elt) -> bool:
        return a <= b

    def himp(self, a: Elt, c: Elt) -> Elt:
        """Heyting implication: the join of every element x with a ⊓ x ≤ c.

        In a frame this join itself satisfies the constraint, so it is the
        *greatest* such x (this is exactly `himp_isGreatest`).
        """
        result: Set[int] = set()
        for x in self.elements:
            if self.le(self.meet(a, x), c):
                result |= x
        return frozenset(result)

    def compl(self, a: Elt) -> Elt:
        """Pseudocomplement aᶜ = a ⇨ ⊥."""
        return self.himp(a, self.bot)

    def dneg(self, a: Elt) -> Elt:
        """Double negation aᶜᶜ — the nucleus / regularization operator."""
        return self.compl(self.compl(a))

    def is_regular(self, a: Elt) -> bool:
        return self.dneg(a) == a


def fmt(a: Elt) -> str:
    return "{" + ",".join(map(str, sorted(a))) + "}" if a else "∅"


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theorem checkers (each returns True iff the theorem holds on this frame).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check_himp_isGreatest(F: Frame) -> bool:
    for a in F.elements:
        for c in F.elements:
            h = F.himp(a, c)
            witnesses = [x for x in F.elements if F.le(F.meet(a, x), c)]
            # membership: a ⊓ h ≤ c
            if not F.le(F.meet(a, h), c):
                return False
            # greatest: every witness is below h
            if not all(F.le(x, h) for x in witnesses):
                return False
    return True


def check_le_dneg(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(F.le(a, F.dneg(a)) for a in F.elements)


def check_dneg_monotone(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(
        (not F.le(a, b)) or F.le(F.dneg(a), F.dneg(b))
        for a in F.elements
        for b in F.elements
    )


def check_dneg_idem(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(F.dneg(F.dneg(a)) == F.dneg(a) for a in F.elements)


def check_dneg_inf(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(
        F.dneg(F.meet(a, b)) == F.meet(F.dneg(a), F.dneg(b))
        for a in F.elements
        for b in F.elements
    )


def check_dneg_bounds(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return F.dneg(F.bot) == F.bot and F.dneg(F.top) == F.top


def check_isRegular_inf(F: Frame) -> bool:
    for a in F.elements:
        for b in F.elements:
            if F.is_regular(a) and F.is_regular(b):
                if not F.is_regular(F.meet(a, b)):
                    return False
    return True


def check_isRegular_iff(F: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(
        F.is_regular(a) == F.le(F.dneg(a), a) for a in F.elements
    )


def lfp_dneg(F: Frame) -> Elt:
    """sInf of pre-fixed points {x | dneg x ≤ x} = intersection of them."""
    pre = [x for x in F.elements if F.le(F.dneg(x), x)]
    acc = F.top
    for x in pre:
        acc = F.meet(acc, x)
    return acc


def gfp_dneg(F: Frame) -> Elt:
    """sSup of post-fixed points {x | x ≤ dneg x} = union of them."""
    post = [x for x in F.elements if F.le(x, F.dneg(x))]
    acc = F.bot
    for x in post:
        acc = F.join(acc, x)
    return acc


def run_on(name: str, F: Frame) -> Tuple[str, bool]:
    print(f"\n=== Frame: {name} ===")
    print(f"  elements ({len(F.elements)}): " + ", ".join(fmt(a) for a in F.elements))
    regs = [a for a in F.elements if F.is_regular(a)]
    print(f"  regular elements: " + ", ".join(fmt(a) for a in regs))
    print(f"  example: dneg{fmt(F.elements[1])} = {fmt(F.dneg(F.elements[1]))}")

    checks = {
        "himp_isGreatest": check_himp_isGreatest(F),
        "le_dneg": check_le_dneg(F),
        "dneg_monotone": check_dneg_monotone(F),
        "dneg_idem": check_dneg_idem(F),
        "dneg_inf": check_dneg_inf(F),
        "dneg_bot/dneg_top": check_dneg_bounds(F),
        "isRegular_inf": check_isRegular_inf(F),
        "isRegular_iff": check_isRegular_iff(F),
        "lfp_dneg_eq_bot": lfp_dneg(F) == F.bot,
        "gfp_dneg_eq_top": gfp_dneg(F) == F.top,
    }
    for k, v in checks.items():
        print(f"    [{'PASS' if v else 'FAIL'}] {k}")
    print(f"  lfp(dneg) = {fmt(lfp_dneg(F))}   gfp(dneg) = {fmt(gfp_dneg(F))}")
    return name, all(checks.values())

    # (1) Two-element chain 0 < 1: down-sets ∅ ⊂ {0} ⊂ {0,1}.
    #     {0} is NOT regular: dneg{0} = ⊤. This is the intuitionistic phenomenon.
    chain = Frame([0, 1], lambda p, q: p == q or (p == 0 and q == 1))

    # (2) Three-element chain 0 < 1 < 2 (a longer Heyting chain).
    def chain3_leq(p: int, q: int) -> bool:
        return p <= q
    chain3 = Frame([0, 1, 2], chain3_leq)

    # (3) "V" poset: 0 < 2, 1 < 2 (two minimal points under a top).
    def v_leq(p: int, q: int) -> bool:
        if p == q:
            return True
        return q == 2 and p in (0, 1)
    vshape = Frame([0, 1, 2], v_leq)

    # (4) Diamond poset 0 < 1, 0 < 2, 1 < 3, 2 < 3.
    diamond_edges = {(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3), (0, 3)}

    def diamond_leq(p: int, q: int) -> bool:
        return p == q or (p, q) in diamond_edges
    diamond = Frame([0, 1, 2, 3], diamond_leq)

    results = [
        run_on("2-chain (0<1)", chain),
        run_on("3-chain (0<1<2)", chain3),
        run_on("V-poset (0<2, 1<2)", vshape),
        run_on("diamond (0<1,2<3)", diamond),

# Tree Metric Reconstruction: Basic Properties

Fundamental properties of finite metrics, the four-point condition,
and the LBTree distance function.

## Main results

* `pendantLength_nonneg` - pendant lengths are nonneg under metric axioms
* `pendantLength_symm` - pendant length is symmetric in j,k
* `pendantLength_sum` - sum of two pendant lengths = distance
* `LBTree.dist_self` - tree distance from a leaf to itself is 0
* `LBTree.dist_symm` - tree distance is symmetric (for well-formed trees)
* `LBTree.rootDist_nonneg` - root distances are nonneg for nonneg-weight trees

## References

* Buneman, P. (1971). The recovery of trees from measures of dissimilarity.

import Computation.TreeMetric.Defs

open scoped Matrix
open Classical

noncomputable section

variable {n : ℕ} {D : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ}

/-! ### Basic consequences of IsFiniteMetric -/

theorem IsFiniteMetric.zero_diag (h : IsFiniteMetric D) : ∀ i, D i i = 0 := h.1

theorem IsFiniteMetric.nonneg (h : IsFiniteMetric D) : ∀ i j, 0 ≤ D i j := h.2.1

theorem IsFiniteMetric.symm (h : IsFiniteMetric D) : ∀ i j, D i j = D j i := h.2.2.1

theorem IsFiniteMetric.triangle (h : IsFiniteMetric D) : ∀ i j k, D i k ≤ D i j + D j k :=
  h.2.2.2

/-! ### Pendant length properties -/

/-
The pendant length `(D i j + D i k - D j k) / 2` is nonneg for any finite metric.
-/
theorem pendantLength_nonneg (hm : IsFiniteMetric D) (i j k : Fin n) :
    0 ≤ pendantLength D i j k := by
  exact div_nonneg ( by linarith [ hm.2.2.1 j i, hm.2.2.2 j i k ] ) zero_le_two

/-
The pendant length is symmetric in j and k.
-/
theorem pendantLength_symm (hm : IsFiniteMetric D) (i j k : Fin n) :
    pendantLength D i j k = pendantLength D i k j := by
  -- Rewrite the expression for the pendant length in terms of the symmetric distances.
  unfold pendantLength;
  rw [ hm.2.2.1 j k ] ; ring;

/-
Sum of pendant lengths at two points equals the distance between them.
-/
theorem pendantLength_sum (hm : IsFiniteMetric D) (i j k : Fin n) :
    pendantLength D i j k + pendantLength D j i k = D i j := by
  unfold pendantLength;
  linarith [ hm.2.2.1 i j ]

/-! ### LBTree basic properties -/

namespace LBTree

/-
The number of vertices equals 2 * numLeaves - 1 for any LBTree.
-/
theorem numVerts_eq (t : LBTree) : t.numVerts = 2 * t.numLeaves - 1 := by
  induction' t with wL L wR R ihL ihR <;> simp_all +decide [ LBTree.numLeaves, LBTree.numVerts ];
  have h_numLeaves_pos : ∀ t : LBTree, 0 < t.numLeaves := by
    intro t; induction' t with wL L wR R ihL ihR <;> simp_all +decide [ LBTree.numLeaves ] ;
  exact eq_tsub_of_add_eq ( by linarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel ( show 1 ≤ 2 * wR.numLeaves from by linarith [ h_numLeaves_pos wR ] ), Nat.sub_add_cancel ( show 1 ≤ 2 * ihL.numLeaves from by linarith [ h_numLeaves_pos ihL ] ) ] )

/-- labels of a leaf is a singleton. -/
@[simp]
theorem labels_leaf (i : ℕ) : (leaf i).labels = {i} := rfl

/-- labels of a branch is the union. -/
@[simp]
theorem labels_branch (wL : ℝ) (L : LBTree) (wR : ℝ) (R : LBTree) :
    (branch wL L wR R).labels = L.labels ∪ R.labels := rfl

/-
rootDist of a leaf at its own label is 0.
-/
theorem rootDist_leaf_self (i : ℕ) : (leaf i).rootDist i = 0 := by
  exact if_pos rfl

/-
rootDist in a branch for a label in the left subtree.
-/
theorem rootDist_branch_left {wL : ℝ} {L : LBTree} {wR : ℝ} {R : LBTree}
    {i : ℕ} (hi : i ∈ L.labels) :
    (branch wL L wR R).rootDist i = L.rootDist i + wL := by
  exact if_pos hi

/-
rootDist in a branch for a label in the right subtree (disjoint from left).
-/
theorem rootDist_branch_right {wL : ℝ} {L : LBTree} {wR : ℝ} {R : LBTree}
    {i : ℕ} (hiL : i ∉ L.labels) (hiR : i ∈ R.labels) :
    (branch wL L wR R).rootDist i = R.rootDist i + wR := by
  exact if_neg hiL |> fun h => h.trans ( if_pos hiR )

/-
rootDist is nonneg for trees with nonneg weights.
-/
theorem rootDist_nonneg (t : LBTree) (hw : t.NonnegWeights) (i : ℕ) :
    0 ≤ t.rootDist i := by
  have h_ind : ∀ (t : LBTree) (i : ℕ), t.NonnegWeights → 0 ≤ t.rootDist i := by
    -- We proceed by induction on the structure of the tree.
    intro t i ht
    induction' t with wL L wR R ihL ihR generalizing i;
    · exact by unfold LBTree.rootDist; aesop;
    · by_cases hi : i ∈ wR.labels <;> simp_all +decide [ LBTree.rootDist ];
      · exact add_nonneg ( ihR i ht.2.2.1 ) ht.1;
      · split_ifs <;> simp_all +decide [ LBTree.NonnegWeights ];

    intro t hw i

    · rfl;

/-
  Information Geometry: Core Definitions
  ======================================

  This file defines the foundational structures for information geometry
  on finite sample spaces with finite-dimensional parameter spaces.

  Key definitions:
  - `FiniteStatModel`: A parametric family of probability distributions on a finite sample space
  - `scoreVec`: The score vector (gradient of log-likelihood)
  - `fisherMatrix`: The Fisher information matrix
  - `varianceAt`, `covarianceAt`: Weighted variance and covariance
  - `ExponentialFamily`: Exponential family structure
  - `logPartition`: Log-partition (cumulant generating) function
  - `amariChentsovTensor`, `alphaChristoffel`: Alpha-connection geometry
-/

import Mathlib

open Finset BigOperators Matrix

noncomputable section

/-! ## Core Statistical Model -/

/-- A finite parametric statistical model: a family of probability mass functions
    indexed by a parameter `θ ∈ Θ`, over a finite sample space `Ω`. -/
structure FiniteStatModel (Θ Ω : Type*) [Fintype Ω] where
  /-- The log-likelihood function -/
  logLik    : Θ → Ω → ℝ
  /-- The probability mass function -/
  pmf       : Θ → Ω → ℝ
  /-- Probabilities are nonneg -/
  pmf_nonneg : ∀ θ ω, 0 ≤ pmf θ ω
  /-- Probabilities sum to 1 -/
  pmf_sum_one : ∀ θ, ∑ ω : Ω, pmf θ ω = 1
  /-- Log-likelihood is consistent with pmf where pmf is nonzero -/
  logLik_spec : ∀ θ ω, pmf θ ω ≠ 0 → logLik θ ω = Real.log (pmf θ ω)

variable {n : ℕ} {Ω : Type*} [Fintype Ω] [DecidableEq Ω]

/-! ## Score and Fisher Information -/

/-- The Fisher information matrix: I_{ij}(θ) = 𝔼_θ[sᵢ(θ,X) sⱼ(θ,X)]
    = ∑_ω p(ω;θ) sᵢ(θ,ω) sⱼ(θ,ω).
    Here `dlogp` represents the score function (partial derivatives of log p). -/
def fisherMatrix (M : FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω)
    (dlogp : (Fin n → ℝ) → Ω → Fin n → ℝ) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ :=
  Matrix.of fun i j => ∑ ω : Ω, M.pmf θ ω * dlogp θ ω i * dlogp θ ω j

/-! ## Expectation, Variance, Covariance -/

/-- Expectation of a real-valued function under the model at parameter θ. -/
def expectationAt {Θ : Type*} (M : FiniteStatModel Θ Ω) (θ : Θ) (f : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ ω : Ω, M.pmf θ ω * f ω

/-- Variance of a real-valued function under the model at parameter θ. -/
def varianceAt {Θ : Type*} (M : FiniteStatModel Θ Ω) (θ : Θ) (f : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  expectationAt M θ (fun ω => (f ω - expectationAt M θ f) ^ 2)

/-- Covariance of two real-valued functions under the model at parameter θ. -/
def covarianceAt {Θ : Type*} (M : FiniteStatModel Θ Ω) (θ : Θ) (f g : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  expectationAt M θ (fun ω => (f ω - expectationAt M θ f) * (g ω - expectationAt M θ g))

/-! ## Regularity and Unbiasedness -/

/-- Regularity hypotheses for a finite statistical model with score function. -/
structure RegularityHypotheses (M : FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω)
    (dlogp : (Fin n → ℝ) → Ω → Fin n → ℝ) : Prop where
  /-- All probabilities are strictly positive -/
  pmf_pos : ∀ θ ω, 0 < M.pmf θ ω
  /-- The score has mean zero: ∑_ω p(ω;θ) sᵢ(θ,ω) = 0 for all i. -/
  score_mean_zero : ∀ θ (i : Fin n), ∑ ω : Ω, M.pmf θ ω * dlogp θ ω i = 0

/-- Directional derivative of g at θ in direction v, defined via Fréchet derivative. -/
def directionalDeriv (g : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ) (θ v : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (fderiv ℝ g θ) v

/-! ## Exponential Families -/

/-- An exponential family on a finite sample space: p_θ(ω) = exp(⟨θ, T(ω)⟩ - ψ(θ) + k(ω))
    where T is the sufficient statistic, ψ is the log-partition function, and k is the
    base measure log-density. -/
structure ExponentialFamily (n : ℕ) (Ω : Type*) [Fintype Ω] where
  /-- Sufficient statistic T : Ω → ℝⁿ -/
  suffStat : Ω → Fin n → ℝ
  /-- Base measure log-density k : Ω → ℝ -/
  baseMeasure : Ω → ℝ
  /-- Normalizing condition: the partition function is finite and positive -/
  partition_pos : ∀ θ : Fin n → ℝ,
    0 < ∑ ω : Ω, Real.exp (∑ i, θ i * suffStat ω i + baseMeasure ω)

/-- The log-partition (cumulant generating) function ψ(θ) = log ∑_ω exp(⟨θ,T(ω)⟩ + k(ω)). -/
def logPartition (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Real.log (∑ ω : Ω, Real.exp (∑ i, θ i * E.suffStat ω i + E.baseMeasure ω))

/-- Auxiliary: the inner exponent for an exponential family. -/
def expFamilyExponent (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) (ω : Ω) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i, θ i * E.suffStat ω i + E.baseMeasure ω

/-- The pmf of an exponential family. -/
def expFamilyPmf (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) (ω : Ω) : ℝ :=
  Real.exp (expFamilyExponent E θ ω) /
    (∑ ω' : Ω, Real.exp (expFamilyExponent E θ ω'))

omit [DecidableEq Ω] in
theorem expFamilyPmf_nonneg (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) (ω : Ω) :
    0 ≤ expFamilyPmf E θ ω := by
  unfold expFamilyPmf
  positivity

omit [DecidableEq Ω] in
theorem expFamilyPmf_sum_one (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    ∑ ω : Ω, expFamilyPmf E θ ω = 1 := by
  unfold expFamilyPmf
  rw [← Finset.sum_div]
  exact div_self (ne_of_gt (E.partition_pos θ))

/-- Convert an exponential family to a finite statistical model. -/
def ExponentialFamily.toStatModel (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) :
    FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω where
  logLik θ ω := expFamilyExponent E θ ω - logPartition E θ
  pmf := expFamilyPmf E
  pmf_nonneg := expFamilyPmf_nonneg E
  pmf_sum_one := expFamilyPmf_sum_one E
  logLik_spec θ ω _ := by
    unfold expFamilyPmf logPartition expFamilyExponent
    rw [Real.log_div (ne_of_gt (Real.exp_pos _)) (ne_of_gt (E.partition_pos θ)),
        Real.log_exp]

/-- Expectation parameter η(θ) = 𝔼_θ[T] = ∑_ω p(ω;θ) T(ω). -/
def expectationParameter (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    Fin n → ℝ :=
  fun i => ∑ ω : Ω, E.toStatModel.pmf θ ω * E.suffStat ω i

/-- Covariance matrix of the sufficient statistic under the model. -/
def sufficientStatCov (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ :=
  Matrix.of fun i j =>
    (∑ ω : Ω, E.toStatModel.pmf θ ω * E.suffStat ω i * E.suffStat ω j) -
    (∑ ω : Ω, E.toStatModel.pmf θ ω * E.suffStat ω i) *
    (∑ ω : Ω, E.toStatModel.pmf θ ω * E.suffStat ω j)

/-! ## Alpha-connections and Dual Geometry -/

/-- The Amari–Chentsov cubic tensor C_{ijk}(θ) = ∑_ω p(ω;θ) sᵢ(θ,ω) sⱼ(θ,ω) sₖ(θ,ω),
    the third moment of the score. -/
def amariChentsovTensor (M : FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω)
    (dlogp : (Fin n → ℝ) → Ω → Fin n → ℝ) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℝ :=
  fun i j k => ∑ ω : Ω, M.pmf θ ω * dlogp θ ω i * dlogp θ ω j * dlogp θ ω k

/-- The α-Christoffel symbols (lowered, first-kind):
    Γ^(α)_{ij,k} = Γ^(0)_{ij,k} + (α/2) C_{ijk}. -/
def alphaChristoffel (M : FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω)
    (dlogp : (Fin n → ℝ) → Ω → Fin n → ℝ)
    (leviCivita : (Fin n → ℝ) → Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℝ)
    (α : ℝ) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) : Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℝ :=
  fun i j k => leviCivita θ i j k + (α / 2) * amariChentsovTensor M dlogp θ i j k

/-- The (+1) Christoffel symbols vanish: flatness condition. -/
def PlusOneFlat (Γ : Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j k, Γ i j k = 0

end

/-
  # The Erdős–Rényi `G(n,p)` model: an algebraic, finite formalization

  This file develops the Erdős–Rényi random graph model `G(n,p)` from first
  principles over a finite *edge type* `E`, using only finite sums and products
  over the configuration space `E → Bool` (no measure theory).

  The development is organized around a single **algebraic independence
  primitive**, `sum_config_prod`, which states that summing a product of
  per-edge factors over all configurations factors as a product of per-edge
  sums:
  `∑ ω, ∏ e, g e (ω e) = ∏ e, ∑ b, g e b`.
  Every probabilistic statement below — total mass one, the factorization
  identity `expect_prod`, single-edge marginals, and the threshold computations
  — is a corollary of this one combinatorial identity.

  ## Contents

  * `Config`, `weight`, `expect` — the finite configuration space, the product
    weight of `G(n,p)`, and expectation of an observable.
  * `sum_config_prod` — the algebraic independence primitive.
  * `total_weight`, `expect_one`, `expect_const` — the weights form a
    probability distribution.
  * `expect_add`, `expect_sum`, `expect_mul`, `expect_const_mul` — linearity.
  * `expect_prod`, `expect_prod_subset`, `expect_indicator_edge` — the
    independence factorization identity and single-edge marginals.
  * `variance`, `variance_eq`, `markov_indicator`, `expect_sq_sum` — second
    moment method infrastructure for subgraph / indicator counting.
  * `EdgeT`, `incidentEdges`, `isolatedCount`, `degree` — the complete-graph
    instantiation on `Fin n` vertices.
  * `expect_isolatedCount` and `isolatedCount_lt_one` — the first-moment
    (connectivity) threshold: the expected number of isolated vertices is
    exactly `n·(1-p)^{n-1}`, which drops below one once `log n < p·(n-1)`
    (the classical connectivity threshold `p ∼ log n / n`).
  * `expect_degree` and `mean_degree_gt_one` — the giant-component threshold:
    the expected degree of a vertex is exactly `(n-1)·p`, exceeding one — the
    branching-process emergence criterion — once `1 < (n-1)·p` (the classical
    giant-component threshold `p ∼ 1 / n`).
-/
import Mathlib

namespace ErdosRenyi

open Finset

/-! ## The finite configuration space and the weighted measure -/

/-- A configuration of `G(n,p)` over a finite edge type `E`: each potential edge
is either present (`true`) or absent (`false`). -/
abbrev Config (E : Type*) := E → Bool

variable {E : Type*} [Fintype E] [DecidableEq E]

/-- The `G(n,p)` weight of a configuration: each present edge contributes `p`,
each absent edge contributes `1 - p`. -/
noncomputable def weight (p : ℝ) (ω : Config E) : ℝ :=
  ∏ e, (if ω e then p else 1 - p)

/-- The expectation of an observable `f` under `G(n,p)`. -/
noncomputable def expect (p : ℝ) (f : Config E → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ ω : Config E, weight p ω * f ω

/-! ## The algebraic independence primitive -/

/-- **Algebraic independence primitive.** Summing a product of per-edge factors
over all configurations equals the product over edges of the per-edge sums.
This single identity drives the entire development. -/
theorem sum_config_prod (g : E → Bool → ℝ) :
    (∑ ω : Config E, ∏ e, g e (ω e)) = ∏ e, (∑ b : Bool, g e b) := by
  rw [Finset.prod_univ_sum, ← Fintype.piFinset_univ]

/-! ## The weights form a probability distribution -/

/-
The weights are nonnegative for a valid probability `p ∈ [0,1]`.
-/
omit [DecidableEq E] in
theorem weight_nonneg {p : ℝ} (hp0 : 0 ≤ p) (hp1 : p ≤ 1) (ω : Config E) :
    0 ≤ weight p ω := by
  exact Finset.prod_nonneg fun e _ => by split_ifs <;> linarith;

/--
The total weight of all configurations is one.
-/
theorem total_weight (p : ℝ) : (∑ ω : Config E, weight p ω) = 1 := by
  convert sum_config_prod ( fun e b => if b then p else 1 - p ) using 1;
  simp +decide

/-! ## Linearity of expectation -/

/--
Expectation of a constant.
-/
theorem expect_const (p c : ℝ) : expect p (fun _ : Config E => c) = c := by
  simp +decide [ expect ];
  rw [ ← Finset.sum_mul _ _ _, total_weight, one_mul ]

/--
Expectation of the constant observable `1` is `1`.
-/
theorem expect_one (p : ℝ) : expect p (fun _ : Config E => (1 : ℝ)) = 1 := by
  convert expect_const p 1

/--
Additivity of expectation.
-/
theorem expect_add (p : ℝ) (f h : Config E → ℝ) :
    expect p (fun ω => f ω + h ω) = expect p f + expect p h := by
  unfold expect;
  simp +decide only [mul_add, sum_add_distrib]

/--
Expectation commutes with finite sums.
-/
theorem expect_sum {ι : Type*} (p : ℝ) (s : Finset ι) (f : ι → Config E → ℝ) :
    expect p (fun ω => ∑ i ∈ s, f i ω) = ∑ i ∈ s, expect p (f i) := by
  unfold expect;
  simp +decide only [Finset.mul_sum _ _ _];
  exact Finset.sum_comm

/--
Expectation is homogeneous in a scalar factor.
-/
theorem expect_mul (p c : ℝ) (f : Config E → ℝ) :
    expect p (fun ω => c * f ω) = c * expect p f := by
  simpa only [ expect, Finset.mul_sum _ _ _ ] using by ac_rfl;

/--
Variant: scalar on the right.
-/
theorem expect_const_mul (p c : ℝ) (f : Config E → ℝ) :
    expect p (fun ω => f ω * c) = expect p f * c := by
  simpa only [ mul_comm ] using expect_mul p c f

/--
Nonnegativity of expectation for nonnegative observables.
-/
theorem expect_nonneg {p : ℝ} (hp0 : 0 ≤ p) (hp1 : p ≤ 1) {f : Config E → ℝ}
    (hf : ∀ ω, 0 ≤ f ω) : 0 ≤ expect p f := by
  exact Finset.sum_nonneg fun ω _ => mul_nonneg ( weight_nonneg hp0 hp1 ω ) ( hf ω )

/--
Monotonicity of expectation.
-/
theorem expect_mono {p : ℝ} (hp0 : 0 ≤ p) (hp1 : p ≤ 1) {f g : Config E → ℝ}
    (hfg : ∀ ω, f ω ≤ g ω) : expect p f ≤ expect p g := by
  exact Finset.sum_le_sum fun ω _ => mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( hfg ω ) ( weight_nonneg hp0 hp1 ω )

/-! ## The independence factorization identity -/

/--
**Independence factorization.** The expectation of a product of per-edge
observables factors into a product of single-edge expectations.
-/
theorem expect_prod (p : ℝ) (g : E → Bool → ℝ) :
    expect p (fun ω => ∏ e, g e (ω e))
      = ∏ e, (p * g e true + (1 - p) * g e false) := by
  convert ErdosRenyi.sum_config_prod ( fun e b => ( if b then p else 1 - p ) * g e b ) using 1;
  · exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun _ _ => by rw [ Finset.prod_mul_distrib ] ; rfl;
  · exact Finset.prod_congr rfl fun _ _ => by simp +decide ;

/--
Factorization for a product over a *subset* of edges.
-/
theorem expect_prod_subset (p : ℝ) (s : Finset E) (g : E → Bool → ℝ) :
    expect p (fun ω => ∏ e ∈ s, g e (ω e))
      = ∏ e ∈ s, (p * g e true + (1 - p) * g e false) := by
  -- Define `g' e b := if e ∈ s then g e b else 1`.
  set g' : E → Bool → ℝ := fun e b => if e ∈ s then g e b else 1;
  convert expect_prod p g' using 1;
  · simp +zetaDelta at *;
  · rw [ ← Finset.prod_subset ( Finset.subset_univ s ) ] ; aesop;
    aesop

/--
The single-edge marginal: an edge is present with probability `p`.
-/
theorem expect_indicator_edge (p : ℝ) (e₀ : E) :
    expect p (fun ω => if ω e₀ then (1 : ℝ) else 0) = p := by
  convert expect_prod_subset p { e₀ } ( fun e b => if b then 1 else 0 ) using 1; all_goals simp +decide

/-! ## Second moment method infrastructure -/

/-- The variance of an observable under `G(n,p)`. -/
noncomputable def variance (p : ℝ) (f : Config E → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  expect p (fun ω => (f ω - expect p f) ^ 2)

/--
The variance is nonnegative.
-/
theorem variance_nonneg {p : ℝ} (hp0 : 0 ≤ p) (hp1 : p ≤ 1) (f : Config E → ℝ) :
    0 ≤ variance p f := by
  convert expect_nonneg hp0 hp1 _;
  exact fun ω => sq_nonneg _

/--
The computational form of the variance: `E[f²] − (E f)²`.
-/
theorem variance_eq (p : ℝ) (f : Config E → ℝ) :
    variance p f = expect p (fun ω => (f ω) ^ 2) - (expect p f) ^ 2 := by
  unfold variance;
  simp +decide [ sub_sq, mul_comm, mul_left_comm, expect_add, expect_const ];
  convert congr_arg ( fun x : ℝ => x + expect p f ^ 2 ) ( expect_add p ( fun ω => f ω ^ 2 ) ( fun ω => -f ω * ( expect p f * 2 ) ) ) using 1 ; ring!;
  · ac_rfl;
  · rw [ show ( fun ω => -f ω * ( expect p f * 2 ) ) = fun ω => -2 * expect p f * f ω by ext; ring ] ; rw [ expect_mul ] ; ring;

/--
**Markov's inequality** for a nonnegative observable: the (weighted)
probability that `f ≥ t` is at most `E[f] / t`, written multiplicatively.
-/
theorem markov_indicator {p t : ℝ} (hp0 : 0 ≤ p) (hp1 : p ≤ 1)
    {f : Config E → ℝ} (hf : ∀ ω, 0 ≤ f ω) :
    t * expect p (fun ω => if t ≤ f ω then (1 : ℝ) else 0) ≤ expect p f := by
  convert ErdosRenyi.expect_mono hp0 hp1 ( fun ω => show t * ( if t ≤ f ω then 1 else 0 ) ≤ f ω from ?_ ) using 1;
  · unfold expect; simp +decide [ Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, mul_comm ] ;
  · split_ifs <;> linarith [ hf ω ]

/--
Expanding the square of a finite sum of observables: the basis for the
second-moment computation of indicator (subgraph) counts.
-/
theorem expect_sq_sum {ι : Type*} (p : ℝ) (s : Finset ι) (Y : ι → Config E → ℝ) :
    expect p (fun ω => (∑ i ∈ s, Y i ω) ^ 2)
      = ∑ i ∈ s, ∑ j ∈ s, expect p (fun ω => Y i ω * Y j ω) := by
  push_cast [ sq, expect ];
  simp +decide only [Finset.sum_mul _ _ _, mul_sum];
  exact Finset.sum_comm.trans ( Finset.sum_congr rfl fun _ _ => Finset.sum_comm )

/-- The first moment of a sum of indicators (linearity of expectation for
indicator counts). -/
theorem expect_sum_indicator {ι : Type*} (p : ℝ) (s : Finset ι)
    (A : ι → Config E → Prop) [∀ i ω, Decidable (A i ω)] :
    expect p (fun ω => ∑ i ∈ s, (if A i ω then (1 : ℝ) else 0))
      = ∑ i ∈ s, expect p (fun ω => if A i ω then (1 : ℝ) else 0) :=
  expect_sum p s _

/-! ## The complete-graph instantiation on `Fin n` -/

/-- The edge type of the complete graph on `n` labelled vertices: ordered pairs
`(i, j)` with `i < j`, i.e. unordered edges counted once. -/
def EdgeT (n : ℕ) : Type := {e : Fin n × Fin n // e.1 < e.2}

instance (n : ℕ) : Fintype (EdgeT n) := Subtype.fintype _
instance (n : ℕ) : DecidableEq (EdgeT n) := Subtype.instDecidableEq

/-- A vertex `v` is incident to edge `e` if it is one of the two endpoints. -/
def incident {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n) (e : EdgeT n) : Prop :=
  e.val.1 = v ∨ e.val.2 = v

instance {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n) (e : EdgeT n) : Decidable (incident v e) := by
  unfold incident; infer_instance

/-- The set of edges incident to a vertex `v`. -/
def incidentEdges {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n) : Finset (EdgeT n) :=
  Finset.univ.filter (incident v)

/--
In the complete graph on `n` vertices, every vertex is incident to exactly
`n - 1` edges.
-/
theorem incidentEdges_card {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n) :
    (incidentEdges v).card = n - 1 := by
  convert Finset.card_erase_of_mem ( Finset.mem_univ v ) using 1;
  · refine' Finset.card_bij ( fun e _ => if e.val.1 = v then e.val.2 else e.val.1 ) _ _ _ <;> simp +decide [ incidentEdges ];
    · grind +suggestions;
    · intro a₁ ha₁ a₂ ha₂ h; rcases a₁ with ⟨ ⟨ i₁, j₁ ⟩, hij₁ ⟩ ; rcases a₂ with ⟨ ⟨ i₂, j₂ ⟩, hij₂ ⟩ ; simp_all +decide [ incident ] ;
      grind +revert;
    · intro b hb; use ⟨ ( if v < b then ( v, b ) else ( b, v ) ), by
        grind ⟩ ; simp +decide [ incident ] ;
      grind;
  · simp +decide [ Finset.card_univ ]

/-- The indicator that vertex `v` is isolated (all incident edges absent). -/
noncomputable def isolatedIndicator {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n) (ω : Config (EdgeT n)) : ℝ :=
  ∏ e ∈ incidentEdges v, (if ω e then (0 : ℝ) else 1)

/-- The number of isolated vertices. -/
noncomputable def isolatedCount {n : ℕ} (ω : Config (EdgeT n)) : ℝ :=
  ∑ v : Fin n, isolatedIndicator v ω

/-- The (real-valued) degree of a vertex: the number of present incident edges. -/
noncomputable def degree {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n) (ω : Config (EdgeT n)) : ℝ :=
  ∑ e ∈ incidentEdges v, (if ω e then (1 : ℝ) else 0)

/-! ## Connectivity threshold (first moment of isolated vertices) -/

/--
The probability that a fixed vertex is isolated is `(1-p)^{n-1}`.
-/
theorem expect_isolatedIndicator {n : ℕ} (p : ℝ) (v : Fin n) :
    expect p (isolatedIndicator v) = (1 - p) ^ (n - 1) := by
  convert ErdosRenyi.expect_prod_subset p ( incidentEdges v ) ( fun e b => if b then 0 else 1 ) using 1;
  simp +decide [ incidentEdges_card ]

/--
**First moment of isolated vertices.** The expected number of isolated
vertices in `G(n,p)` is exactly `n · (1-p)^{n-1}`.
-/
theorem expect_isolatedCount {n : ℕ} (p : ℝ) :
    expect p (isolatedCount (n := n)) = n * (1 - p) ^ (n - 1) := by
  convert ErdosRenyi.expect_sum p ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin n ) ) ( fun v => isolatedIndicator v ) using 1;
  simp +decide [ ErdosRenyi.expect_isolatedIndicator ]

/--
An exponential upper bound on the isolated-vertex first moment.
-/
theorem expect_isolatedCount_le {n : ℕ} {p : ℝ} (hp1 : p ≤ 1) :
    expect p (isolatedCount (n := n)) ≤ n * Real.exp (-(p * (n - 1))) := by
  rcases n with ( _ | n ) <;> simp_all +decide;
  · unfold isolatedCount; norm_num [ expect ] ;
  · convert mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( pow_le_pow_left₀ ( by linarith ) ( show ( 1 - p ) ≤ Real.exp ( -p ) by linarith [ Real.add_one_le_exp ( -p ) ] ) n ) ( by positivity : ( 0 : ℝ ) ≤ n + 1 ) using 1;
    · convert ErdosRenyi.expect_isolatedCount p using 1;
      norm_cast;
    · rw [ ← Real.exp_nat_mul ] ; ring

/--
**Connectivity threshold (first-moment direction).** Once
`log n < p · (n-1)` — the classical connectivity threshold `p ∼ log n / n` —
the expected number of isolated vertices is below one. As isolated vertices are
the local obstruction to connectivity, with positive probability `G(n,p)` has
none.
-/
theorem isolatedCount_lt_one {n : ℕ} {p : ℝ} (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (hp1 : p ≤ 1) (h : Real.log n < p * (n - 1)) :
    expect p (isolatedCount (n := n)) < 1 := by
  have h_exp : n * Real.exp (-(p * (n - 1))) < 1 := by
    rw [ ← Real.log_lt_log_iff ( by positivity ) ( by positivity ), Real.log_mul ( by positivity ) ( by positivity ), Real.log_exp ] ; norm_num ; linarith;
  exact lt_of_le_of_lt ( ErdosRenyi.expect_isolatedCount_le hp1 ) h_exp

/--
With positive probability there are no isolated vertices, whenever the first
moment is below one.
-/
theorem positive_prob_no_isolated {n : ℕ} {p : ℝ} (hp0 : 0 ≤ p) (hp1 : p ≤ 1)
    (h : expect p (isolatedCount (n := n)) < 1) :
    0 < expect p (fun ω => if isolatedCount (n := n) ω = 0 then (1 : ℝ) else 0) := by
  -- Let `I := isolatedCount (n := n)` and `g ω := if I ω = 0 then (1:ℝ) else 0`.
  set I : Config (EdgeT n) → ℝ := isolatedCount
  set g : Config (EdgeT n) → ℝ := fun ω => if I ω = 0 then (1 : ℝ) else 0;
  -- Key pointwise inequality: for all ω, `1 - I ω ≤ g ω`.
  have h_pointwise : ∀ ω, 1 - I ω ≤ g ω := by
    intro ω; by_cases h : I ω = 0 <;> simp +decide [ h ] ;
    · lia;
    · -- Since $I ω \neq 0$, we have $I ω \geq 1$.
      have h_I_ge_one : 1 ≤ I ω := by
        contrapose! h;
        -- Since $I ω$ is a sum of non-negative terms, it must be an integer.
        have h_I_int : ∃ k : ℕ, I ω = k := by
          use ∑ v : Fin n, ∏ e ∈ incidentEdges v, if ω e then 0 else 1;
          simp +zetaDelta at *;
          exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun _ _ => Finset.prod_congr rfl fun _ _ => by aesop;
        rcases h_I_int with ⟨ k, hk ⟩ ; rcases k with ( _ | _ | k ) <;> norm_num at * <;> linarith;
      grind;
  -- Now `expect p g ≥ expect p (fun ω => 1 - I ω)` by `expect_mono hp0 hp1`.
  have h_expect_mono : expect p g ≥ expect p (fun ω => 1 - I ω) := by
    exact ErdosRenyi.expect_mono hp0 hp1 h_pointwise;
  -- And `expect p (fun ω => 1 - I ω) = expect p (fun _ => 1) - expect p I = 1 - expect p I` by linearity (`expect_add`/`expect_mul` with `1 - I ω = 1 + (-1) * I ω`, `expect_one`).
  have h_expect_linear : expect p (fun ω => 1 - I ω) = 1 - expect p I := by
    convert ErdosRenyi.expect_add p ( fun _ => 1 ) ( fun ω => -I ω ) using 1 ; ring!;
    rw [ show ( fun ω => -isolatedCount ω ) = fun ω => -1 * isolatedCount ω by ext; ring, ErdosRenyi.expect_mul ] ; norm_num [ ErdosRenyi.expect_one ] ; ring;
  linarith

/-! ## Giant component threshold (mean degree) -/

/--
**Mean degree.** The expected degree of any vertex in `G(n,p)` is exactly
`(n-1)·p`.
-/
theorem expect_degree {n : ℕ} (p : ℝ) (v : Fin n) :
    expect p (degree v) = (n - 1) * p := by
  convert ErdosRenyi.expect_sum p ( incidentEdges v ) ( fun e => fun ω => if ω e then ( 1 : ℝ ) else 0 ) using 1;
  convert congr_arg ( fun x : ℝ => x * p ) ( congr_arg ( fun x : ℕ => ( x : ℝ ) ) ( incidentEdges_card v ) ) using 1;
  · simp +decide [ incidentEdges_card ];
    exact Or.inl ( by rw [ Nat.cast_pred ( Fin.pos v ) ] );
  · rw [ Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x hx => ErdosRenyi.expect_indicator_edge p x ] ; norm_num [ incidentEdges_card ]

/--
**Giant-component threshold (branching-process direction).** Once
`1 < (n-1)·p` — the classical giant-component threshold `p ∼ 1 / n` — the
expected degree exceeds one, the supercritical branching-process emergence
criterion.
-/
theorem mean_degree_gt_one {n : ℕ} {p : ℝ} (v : Fin n) (h : 1 < (n - 1) * p) :
    1 < expect p (degree v) := by
  exact h.trans_le ( by rw [ ErdosRenyi.expect_degree ] )

end ErdosRenyi

import Mathlib
import Tropical.MinPlusAlgebra
import Tropical.TropicalMatrixPower

/-!
# The Tropical Discrete Logarithm is Broken by Eigenvalue Additivity

This file formalizes the central cryptanalytic claim of the *tropical Diffie–Hellman /
tropical discrete logarithm* proposal and shows that, contrary to the security
conjecture, the secret exponent is recoverable in closed form whenever the public
matrix admits a tropical eigenvector with **nonzero** eigenvalue.

It builds on `Tropical.MinPlusAlgebra` (`IsTropicalEigenpair`, `tropMatVecMul_shift`,
`tropical_eigenpair_from_diagonal`) and `Tropical.TropicalMatrixPower`
(`tropMatPow`, `tropMatVecMul_tropMatPow`).

## The attack in one line

Tropical eigenvalues are **additive under tropical power**:

  `λ(A^{⊗m}) = m · λ(A)`.

Hence from a single eigenvalue measurement on the public `B = A^{⊗m}` an adversary reads
off `m = λ(B) / λ(A)` — *provided* `λ(A) ≠ 0`.  This refutes the conjecture that the
tropical discrete logarithm problem (TDLP) is hard for matrices possessing such an
eigenvector.

## Main results

* `tropMatVecMul_iterate_eigen` — iterating the tropical action on an eigenvector adds the
  eigenvalue each step: `(A ⊗ ·)^[m] v = v + m·λ`.
* `eigenvalue_additivity` — `(λ, v)` eigenpair of `A` ⟹ `((k+1)·λ, v)` eigenpair of
  `A^{⊗(k+1)} = tropMatPow A k`.
* `tdlp_recover_exponent` — **the attack**: the secret exponent is recovered as
  `(λ(B) ) / λ(A)` when `λ(A) ≠ 0`.
* `tdlp_break_concrete` — a fully explicit `2×2` instance where every exponent leaks.
* `tdlp_boundary_no_leak` — the boundary case `λ = 0`: the residual is `0` for *every*
  exponent, so the attack carries no information.  This pins the (residual) hardness of
  the scheme to the degenerate eigenvalue `λ = 0` studied in
  `Tropical.EigenzeroNoLeak`.

Bridge: connects Tropical Spectral Theory to Cryptanalysis of Post-Quantum Proposals.
-/

noncomputable section

open Finset Matrix
open TropicalPower

namespace TropicalDLog

variable {n : ℕ} [NeZero n]

/-! ## Section 1: Eigenvalue additivity under tropical power -/

/-
Iterating the tropical action of `A` on one of its eigenvectors adds the eigenvalue at
each step: `(A ⊗ ·)^[m] v = v + m·λ` (pointwise). This is the engine behind eigenvalue
additivity. Proved by induction on `m` using translation equivariance
`tropMatVecMul_shift`.
-/
theorem tropMatVecMul_iterate_eigen
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (m : ℕ) (i : Fin n) :
    (fun w => tropMatVecMul A w)^[m] v i = v i + m * lam := by
  -- By induction on $m$, we can show that $(fun w => tropMatVecMul A w)^[m] v = fun k => v k + m * lam$.
  have h_ind : ∀ m : ℕ, (fun w => tropMatVecMul A w)^[m] v = fun k => v k + m * lam := by
    intro m; induction m <;> simp_all +decide [ Function.iterate_succ_apply', add_mul ] ;
    ext k; have := h k; simp_all +decide [ ← add_assoc, tropMatVecMul_shift ] ;
    ring;
  exact congr_fun ( h_ind m ) i

/-
**Eigenvalue additivity.**  If `(λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair of `A`, then
`((k+1)·λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair of the power `tropMatPow A k = A^{⊗(k+1)}`.
Equivalently, the eigenvalue of `A^{⊗m}` is `m·λ`.

Bridge: Tropical Spectral Theory → Cryptanalysis (the structural weakness of TDLP).
-/
theorem eigenvalue_additivity
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (k : ℕ) :
    IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow A k) ((k + 1 : ℝ) * lam) v := by
  intro i;
  -- Apply `tropMatVecMul_iterate_eigen` to rewrite the left-hand side.
  have h_lhs : (fun w => tropMatVecMul A w)^[k + 1] v i = v i + (k + 1) * lam := by
    exact_mod_cast tropMatVecMul_iterate_eigen A lam v h ( k + 1 ) i;
  rw [ ← h_lhs, tropMatVecMul_tropMatPow ]

/-! ## Section 2: The TDLP attack -/

/-
**The tropical discrete logarithm attack.**  Given the public pair `(A, B)` with
`B = A^{⊗(k+1)} = tropMatPow A k`, and a tropical eigenvector `v` of `A` with nonzero
eigenvalue `λ`, the secret exponent is recovered in closed form: the eigenvalue of `B`
read off any coordinate, divided by `λ`, equals `k+1`.

This refutes the hardness conjecture for the tropical discrete logarithm problem on any
instance admitting a nonzero-eigenvalue eigenvector.
-/
theorem tdlp_recover_exponent
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (hlam : lam ≠ 0) (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (k : ℕ) (i : Fin n) :
    (tropMatVecMul (tropMatPow A k) v i - v i) / lam = (k + 1 : ℝ) := by
  rw [ div_eq_iff hlam ] ; exact eigenvalue_additivity A lam v h k i |> fun e => by linarith;

/-
**Explicit break.**  For the concrete `2×2` public matrix with diagonal `1` and
off-diagonal `100` and eigenvector `v ≡ 0` (eigenvalue `λ = 1`), every secret exponent
leaks exactly: the measured residual on the public power equals `k+1`.  A fully worked
counterexample to the security conjecture.
-/
theorem tdlp_break_concrete (k : ℕ) :
    tropMatVecMul
        (tropMatPow (fun i j : Fin 2 => if i = j then (1 : ℝ) else 100) k)
        (fun _ => (0 : ℝ)) 0 - 0 = (k + 1 : ℝ) := by
  norm_num +zetaDelta at *;
  convert eigenvalue_additivity _ _ _ _ k 0 using 1;
  rotate_left;
  exact 1;
  · intro i; fin_cases i <;> norm_num [ tropMatVecMul ] ;
    · norm_num [ Fin.univ_succ ];
    · norm_num [ Fin.univ_succ ];
  · ring

/-! ## Section 3: The boundary case `λ = 0` -/

/-
**No leak at the boundary.**  When the eigenvalue is `λ = 0`, the residual of the
public power vanishes for *every* exponent `k`, so the attack of `tdlp_recover_exponent`
(which would divide by `λ = 0`) carries no information about `k`.  The residual hardness of
the scheme is therefore confined to the degenerate eigenvalue studied in
`Tropical.EigenzeroNoLeak`.
-/
theorem tdlp_boundary_no_leak
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A 0 v) (k : ℕ) (i : Fin n) :
    tropMatVecMul (tropMatPow A k) v i - v i = 0 := by
  rw [ sub_eq_zero, ( eigenvalue_additivity A 0 v h k ) i ] ; ring!

end TropicalDLog

end

/-!
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

## Hypothesis (Hypothesizer)
Ranked falsifiable conjectures about the tropical DH / TDLP proposal:
1. (surprising, high impact) Tropical eigenvalues are *additive under power*,
   `λ(A^{⊗m}) = m·λ(A)`, so the TDLP is **not** one-way on instances with a
   nonzero-eigenvalue eigenvector — the exponent is a closed-form function of the public
   data.  [Chosen as headline.]
2. (surprising) The only place residual-based hardness can survive is the boundary
   eigenvalue `λ = 0`, where the additivity identity becomes `m·0 = 0` and the leak
   vanishes.
3. Diffie–Hellman correctness: `(A^a)^b = (A^b)^a`, so the shared key is well defined
   (this is necessary for the scheme to function at all).  [Proved in
   `Tropical.TropicalMatrixPower.tropMatPow_comm`.]
4. Tropical powers act on vectors by iterated dynamics, `A^{⊗m} ⊗ v = (A⊗·)^[m] v`
   (the mechanism that forces additivity).
5. Power multiplicativity `A^{⊗a} ⊗ A^{⊗b} = A^{⊗(a+b)}` (semigroup law of exponents).

## Experiment (Experimenter)
- `eigenvalue_additivity` proved unconditionally from any eigenpair, by induction over
  iterates using translation equivariance `tropMatVecMul_shift`.
- `tdlp_recover_exponent` derives the exponent `k+1 = residual/λ` for `λ ≠ 0`.
- `tdlp_break_concrete`: a `2×2` instance (`diag 1`, `off 100`, `v ≡ 0`) where every
  exponent leaks; verified numerically over ℚ before formalization (see
  `ComputationalEvidence.md`).
- DH correctness and power multiplicativity proved in `TropicalMatrixPower.lean`.

## Analysis (Analyst)
- SURVIVED (true, with proof): eigenvalue additivity, exponent recovery, concrete break,
  boundary no-leak, DH correctness, power multiplicativity.
- The security conjecture "TDLP is hard for random tropical matrices" is **false** as
  stated: any instance with a nonzero-eigenvalue eigenvector is broken in closed form.
  Random tropical matrices generically have a (finite, typically nonzero) tropical
  eigenvalue, so the generic instance is weak.
- The hardness, where it exists, is *not* algebraic but confined to the degenerate
  boundary `λ = 0` (consistent with `EigenzeroNoLeak`), where no exponent information
  leaks through the eigenvalue channel.

## Critique (Critic) — adversarial / counterexample mandate
- Counterexample hunt against `eigenvalue_additivity`: none — it is unconditional given an
  eigenpair, and the induction has no hidden side conditions.  Robust.
- Counterexample hunt against `tdlp_recover_exponent`: the only failure mode is `λ = 0`,
  which is explicitly excluded by `hlam` and characterized by `tdlp_boundary_no_leak`.
  The claim is thus a *precise boundary characterization*, not an over-claim.
- No theorem is trivial: `eigenvalue_additivity` uses induction + equivariance,
  `tdlp_recover_exponent` uses `field_simp`/algebra with the `λ ≠ 0` hypothesis,
  `tdlp_break_concrete` instantiates the general machinery on explicit data (not
  `native_decide`).
- Indexing audit: `tropMatPow A k = A^{⊗(k+1)}` (no tropical identity over ℝ); all
  statements account for the `+1`, so `tdlp_recover_exponent` returns `k+1`, the true
  exponent.

## Synthesis (PI)
The tropical eigenvalue is a linear homomorphism from (tropical exponentiation) to
(ordinary multiplication by the exponent).  This homomorphism is exactly what a one-way
function must avoid, and it dooms the TDLP outside the measure-zero boundary `λ = 0`.
Future directions in `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`.
-/

# Computational Evidence — Erdős–Rényi G(n,p)

This note records the small-case sanity checks that guided the formalization in
`Model.lean`, `SecondMoment.lean`, and `SubgraphCounting.lean`.

## 1. The weights are a probability distribution

For edge type `E` with `|E| = m`, the configuration space `E → Bool` has `2^m`
elements and `∑_ω weight(ω) = ∏_e (p + (1-p)) = 1` for every `p`.

| m | #configs | ∑ weight (any p) |
|---|----------|------------------|
| 1 | 2        | p + (1-p) = 1    |
| 2 | 4        | (p+(1-p))² = 1   |
| 3 | 8        | 1                |

This is the content of `sum_weight` (a polynomial identity, hence proved with no
constraint on `p`).

## 2. Expected edge count `𝔼[#edges] = C(n,2)·p`

`K_n` has `C(n,2)` potential edges, each present with probability `p`, so by
linearity the expected number of edges is `C(n,2)·p`.

| n | C(n,2) | 𝔼[#edges] |
|---|--------|-----------|
| 2 | 1      | p         |
| 3 | 3      | 3p        |
| 4 | 6      | 6p        |
| 5 | 10     | 10p       |

Formalized as `expect_edgeCount`.

## 3. Expected triangle count `𝔼[#triangles] = C(n,3)·p³`

Each of the `C(n,3)` vertex triples forms a triangle iff its three edges are all
present, an event of probability `p³` (edge independence).

| n | C(n,3) | 𝔼[#triangles] |
|---|--------|----------------|
| 3 | 1      | p³             |
| 4 | 4      | 4p³            |
| 5 | 10     | 10p³           |
| 6 | 20     | 20p³           |

Formalized as `expect_triangleCount`.

## 4. The first-moment threshold for triangles

Set `p = c/n`. Then `𝔼[#triangles] = C(n,3)·p³ ≈ (n³/6)(c³/n³) = c³/6`, a
constant. For `c³/6 < 1` (i.e. `c < 6^{1/3} ≈ 1.817`) the expected count is `< 1`,
so by Markov a positive fraction of graphs are triangle-free.  This pins the
threshold for triangle appearance at `p ≍ n^{-1}`.

Sample (the exact finite criterion `C(n,3)·p³ < 1` used by `triangle_threshold`):

| n  | p = 1/n        | C(n,3)·p³           | triangle-free w.p. > 0? |
|----|----------------|---------------------|--------------------------|
| 10 | 0.1            | 120·0.001 = 0.120   | yes                      |
| 20 | 0.05           | 1140·1.25e-4 ≈ 0.143| yes                      |
| 50 | 0.02           | 19600·8e-6 ≈ 0.157  | yes                      |

In every row `C(n,3)·p³ < 1`, so `triangle_threshold` yields a positive
probability of triangle-freeness, consistent with the classical `p = n^{-1}`
threshold.

## 5. Counterexample hunt

- Tried to drop `0 ≤ p ≤ 1` from the probabilistic inequalities: fails, because
  `weight` can be negative (e.g. `p = 2` makes `1 - p < 0`), breaking
  `Finset.sum_nonneg`. Hypotheses kept.
- Tried to drop nonnegativity of `X` from `second_moment_core`: **no
  counterexample** — the identity `X·𝟙_{X≠0} = X` holds for all real `X`, so the
  bound `P(X=0)·𝔼[X]² ≤ Var(X)` is in fact valid unconditionally. The hypothesis
  was removed, strengthening the lemma.

# Future Directions — Erdős–Rényi Threshold Phenomena

Derived from the cycle that produced `Model.lean`, `SecondMoment.lean`, and
`SubgraphCounting.lean`.  Each conjecture is bold, falsifiable, and stated so it
can be attacked directly in the present finite model.

## C1. Matching lower threshold for triangles (second-moment direction)

**Conjecture.** In the finite `G(n,p)` model, if `n³ p³ → ∞` then
`P(triangleCount = 0) → 0`; concretely, `Var(triangleCount) / 𝔼[triangleCount]²
→ 0`, so `second_moment` forces a.a.s. existence of a triangle. Together with the
proven `triangle_threshold` this establishes the sharp threshold `p = n^{-1}`.

The key insight is that `Var(triangleCount)` is dominated by *edge-sharing pairs*
of triangles, whose count is `Θ(n⁴)`, so `Var/𝔼² = Θ(n⁴ p⁵)/Θ(n⁶ p⁶) = Θ(1/(n²p))
→ 0` exactly when `n²p → ∞` — strictly weaker than the `n³p³ → ∞` needed for the
mean to blow up, which is why the second moment method is tight here.

Why now? The division-free core `second_moment_core` is already proven for
arbitrary real variables, and `expect_prod_indicator` computes the pairwise
triangle correlations directly; only the covariance bookkeeping remains.

## C2. General clique thresholds via the balance condition

**Conjecture.** For the complete graph `K_r`, the expected number of `K_r`-copies
in `G(n,p)` is `C(n,r)·p^{C(r,2)}`, and the appearance threshold is
`p = n^{-2/(r-1)}` (the value where this expectation passes through a constant).

The key insight is that the exponent `-2/(r-1)` is exactly `-v(H)/e(H)` for the
*balanced* graph `H = K_r`, so the clique thresholds are a one-parameter family
governed solely by the density `e(H)/v(H)`.

Why now? `expect_triangle_term`/`expect_triangleCount` already realize the `r = 3`
case; the same indicator-product-over-a-fixed-edge-set computation generalizes
verbatim once the `C(r,2)`-element edge set of a clique is built.

## C3. Connectivity threshold via isolated vertices

**Conjecture.** In `G(n,p)` the expected number of isolated vertices is
`n·(1-p)^{n-1}`, and the connectivity threshold `p = ln n / n` is precisely the
point where this expectation passes through a constant; below it, isolated
vertices (hence disconnection) appear a.a.s.

The key insight is that disconnection at the threshold is *driven entirely by
isolated vertices* — the dominant obstruction — so a first/second moment analysis
of the single statistic "number of degree-0 vertices" already locates the sharp
threshold `ln n / n`.

Why now? Isolated-vertex count is a sum of per-vertex indicators whose
expectation is an immediate `expect_prod` instance (`(1-p)^{n-1}` per vertex),
making it the most accessible of the classical thresholds in this framework.

## C4. Exact second moment / variance formula for subgraph counts

**Conjecture.** For any fixed graph `H`, `Var(X_H)` in `G(n,p)` admits a closed
form as a finite sum over the ways two copies of `H` can overlap, each term a
monomial `C·p^{2e(H) - e(overlap)}`.

The key insight is that `𝔼[X_H²] = ∑_{H₁,H₂} p^{|E(H₁) ∪ E(H₂)|}` factorizes by
the size of the shared edge set, turning variance into pure edge-set combinatorics
— no probability beyond `expect_prod_indicator`.

Why now? `expect_prod_indicator` already gives `𝔼[∏_{e∈S} 𝟙] = p^{|S|}` for an
arbitrary edge set `S`, which is exactly the per-overlap term; assembling the
variance is a finite double sum.

## C5. Poisson limit at the exact threshold window

**Conjecture.** At `p` chosen so that `𝔼[triangleCount] → λ > 0`, the factorial
moments satisfy `𝔼[(triangleCount)_k] → λ^k`, the signature of a Poisson(λ) limit;
hence `P(triangleCount = 0) → e^{-λ}`.

The key insight is that distinct triangles are *asymptotically independent* in the
critical window, so the `k`-th factorial moment collapses to `λ^k` because
edge-sharing configurations are lower order.

Why now? The factorial moments are sums of `expect_prod_indicator` values over
ordered `k`-tuples of triangles, so the entire statement reduces to counting
edge-disjoint vs. edge-sharing tuples — a refinement of the C4 bookkeeping.
