import Mathlib

/-!
# Anti-Gravity Theorems in Finite Theorem-Dependency Libraries

This file develops a small, self-contained *finite dependency calculus* that makes
precise the informal "anti-gravity" intuition: in a finite library of theorems,
some theorems are simultaneously *heavy* (many other theorems depend directly on
them) and *cheap* (they have short proofs).  Such theorems "defy gravity": despite
their short proofs they carry a lot of downstream weight.

We model a library by a finite type of theorem names together with a decidable
direct-dependency relation and a proof-length function.  We define the *weight* of
a theorem as the number of theorems that depend directly on it, and the predicate
`AntiGravity L K B t` saying that `t` has weight at least `K` and proof length at
most `B`.

The main results are:

* `weight_le_card` — weight is bounded by the size of the library;
* `antigravity_mono` — anti-gravity is monotone (weaker thresholds, larger budgets);
* `antigravity_pigeonhole` / `totalWeight_le_of_all_light` — a counting/pigeonhole
  theorem: if the short theorems carry more total weight than `card · (K-1)`, then a
  short heavy (anti-gravity) theorem must exist;
* `DepDense` and `DepDense_mono` — a reflexive-transitive dependency-density notion
  and its monotonicity;
* an explicit `starLibrary` example with one center and `n` leaves, where we compute
  `weight center = n`, exhibit an anti-gravity theorem, and show the anti-gravity set
  is dependency-dense.

Finally `antiGravityCandidates` is an executable `Finset` whose membership is proved
equivalent to `AntiGravity`.
-/

namespace AntiGravityFinite

open Finset

/-- A finite theorem-dependency library: a finite type of theorem names with a
decidable direct-dependency relation and a proof-length function.

`depends u t` reads "theorem `u` depends *directly* on theorem `t`". -/
structure FiniteLibrary where
  /-- The (finite) type of theorem names. -/
  Thm : Type
  /-- `Thm` is finite. -/
  fintypeThm : Fintype Thm
  /-- Equality of theorem names is decidable. -/
  decEqThm : DecidableEq Thm
  /-- Direct dependency relation: `depends u t` means `u` depends directly on `t`. -/
  depends : Thm → Thm → Prop
  /-- The dependency relation is decidable. -/
  decDepends : DecidableRel depends
  /-- The proof length of each theorem. -/
  proofLength : Thm → ℕ

attribute [instance] FiniteLibrary.fintypeThm FiniteLibrary.decEqThm FiniteLibrary.decDepends

variable (L : FiniteLibrary)

/-- The **weight** of a theorem `t`: the number of theorems depending *directly* on `t`. -/
def weight (t : L.Thm) : ℕ := (univ.filter (fun u => L.depends u t)).card

/-- The **anti-gravity** predicate: `t` has weight at least `K` and proof length at most `B`. -/
def AntiGravity (K B : ℕ) (t : L.Thm) : Prop := K ≤ weight L t ∧ L.proofLength t ≤ B

/-- The set of **short** theorems: those with proof length at most `B`. -/
def shortSet (B : ℕ) : Finset L.Thm := univ.filter (fun t => L.proofLength t ≤ B)

/-- The set of **anti-gravity** theorems for thresholds `K` (weight) and `B` (proof length). -/
def antiSet (K B : ℕ) : Finset L.Thm :=
  univ.filter (fun t => K ≤ weight L t ∧ L.proofLength t ≤ B)

/-- The total direct weight carried by all short theorems. -/
def totalWeightOnShort (B : ℕ) : ℕ := ∑ t ∈ shortSet L B, weight L t

/-- Executable list of anti-gravity candidates (definitionally the `antiSet`). -/
def antiGravityCandidates (K B : ℕ) : Finset L.Thm := antiSet L K B

/-! ## Basic theorems -/

/-- The weight of any theorem is bounded by the size of the library. -/
theorem weight_le_card (t : L.Thm) : weight L t ≤ Fintype.card L.Thm := by
  unfold weight
  exact le_trans (card_filter_le _ _) (le_of_eq card_univ)

/-- Anti-gravity is monotone: lowering the weight threshold and raising the
proof-length budget preserves it. -/
theorem antigravity_mono {K K' B B' : ℕ} {t : L.Thm}
    (h : AntiGravity L K B t) (hK : K' ≤ K) (hB : B ≤ B') : AntiGravity L K' B' t :=
  ⟨le_trans hK h.1, le_trans h.2 hB⟩

/-- Membership in the executable candidate set is exactly the anti-gravity predicate. -/
theorem mem_antiGravityCandidates {K B : ℕ} {t : L.Thm} :
    t ∈ antiGravityCandidates L K B ↔ AntiGravity L K B t := by
  unfold antiGravityCandidates antiSet AntiGravity
  rw [mem_filter]
  simp

/-! ## The counting / pigeonhole theorem -/

/-- Contrapositive counting bound: if every short theorem has weight at most `K-1`,
then the total weight on short theorems is at most `card · (K-1)`. -/
theorem totalWeight_le_of_all_light {K B : ℕ}
    (h : ∀ t ∈ shortSet L B, weight L t ≤ K - 1) :
    totalWeightOnShort L B ≤ (shortSet L B).card * (K - 1) := by
  unfold totalWeightOnShort
  calc ∑ t ∈ shortSet L B, weight L t
      ≤ (shortSet L B).card • (K - 1) := Finset.sum_le_card_nsmul _ _ _ h
    _ = (shortSet L B).card * (K - 1) := by rw [smul_eq_mul]

/-- **Pigeonhole / anti-gravity existence theorem.**  If `0 < K` and the short
theorems collectively carry more weight than `card · (K-1)`, then there is a short
theorem of weight at least `K`, i.e. an anti-gravity theorem. -/
theorem antigravity_pigeonhole {K B : ℕ} (hK : 0 < K)
    (h : (shortSet L B).card * (K - 1) < totalWeightOnShort L B) :
    ∃ t, AntiGravity L K B t := by
  by_contra hcon
  push_neg at hcon
  have hlight : ∀ t ∈ shortSet L B, weight L t ≤ K - 1 := by
    intro t ht
    have htlen : L.proofLength t ≤ B := by
      simpa [shortSet, mem_filter] using ht
    have hnot : ¬ (K ≤ weight L t ∧ L.proofLength t ≤ B) := hcon t
    have hw : ¬ (K ≤ weight L t) := fun hk => hnot ⟨hk, htlen⟩
    omega
  have := totalWeight_le_of_all_light L hlight
  omega

/-! ## Dependency density -/

/-- A finite set `A` of theorems is **dependency-dense** if every theorem reaches
some element of `A` along the reflexive-transitive closure of the dependency
relation. -/
def DepDense (A : Finset L.Thm) : Prop :=
  ∀ t, ∃ a, a ∈ A ∧ Relation.ReflTransGen L.depends t a

/-- Density is monotone under enlarging the target set. -/
theorem DepDense_mono {A A' : Finset L.Thm} (hsub : A ⊆ A') (h : DepDense L A) :
    DepDense L A' := by
  intro t
  obtain ⟨a, ha, hr⟩ := h t
  exact ⟨a, hsub ha, hr⟩

end AntiGravityFinite

/-! ## The star library example -/

namespace AntiGravityFinite

open Finset

/-- Theorem names of the star library: one `center` and `n` leaves. -/
inductive StarThm (n : ℕ) where
  | center : StarThm n
  | leaf : Fin n → StarThm n
deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

/-- Dependency in the star library: each leaf depends on the center, nothing else. -/
def starDependsBool (n : ℕ) : StarThm n → StarThm n → Bool
  | .leaf _, .center => true
  | _, _ => false

/-- Proof lengths: the center has proof length `1`, each leaf has proof length `2`. -/
def starProofLength (n : ℕ) : StarThm n → ℕ
  | .center => 1
  | .leaf _ => 2

/-- The explicit star library with one center and `n` leaves. -/
def starLibrary (n : ℕ) : FiniteLibrary where
  Thm := StarThm n
  fintypeThm := inferInstance
  decEqThm := inferInstance
  depends u t := starDependsBool n u t = true
  decDepends := fun _ _ => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (_ = true))
  proofLength := starProofLength n

/-
The set of theorems depending on the center is exactly the set of leaves.
-/
theorem star_weight_center (n : ℕ) : weight (starLibrary n) StarThm.center = n := by
  unfold weight starLibrary;
  convert Finset.card_image_of_injective ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin n ) ) ( show Function.Injective ( fun k : Fin n => StarThm.leaf k ) from ?_ ) using 2;
  · ext ( _ | u ) <;> simp +decide [ starDependsBool ];
  · simp +decide [ Finset.card_univ ];
  · exact fun a b h => by injection h;

/-- The center is an anti-gravity theorem with thresholds `K = n`, `B = 1`. -/
theorem star_antigravity_center (n : ℕ) :
    AntiGravity (starLibrary n) n 1 StarThm.center := by
  refine ⟨(star_weight_center n).ge, ?_⟩
  show starProofLength n StarThm.center ≤ 1
  simp [starProofLength]

/-- The singleton `{center}` is dependency-dense in the star library. -/
theorem star_center_dense (n : ℕ) : DepDense (starLibrary n) {StarThm.center} := by
  intro t
  refine ⟨StarThm.center, mem_singleton_self _, ?_⟩
  cases t with
  | center => exact Relation.ReflTransGen.refl
  | leaf i =>
      exact Relation.ReflTransGen.single (by
        show starDependsBool n (StarThm.leaf i) StarThm.center = true
        rfl)

/-- The center lies in the anti-gravity set for thresholds `K = n`, `B = 1`. -/
theorem star_center_mem_antiSet (n : ℕ) :
    StarThm.center ∈ antiSet (starLibrary n) n 1 := by
  rw [antiSet, mem_filter]
  exact ⟨mem_univ _, star_antigravity_center n⟩

/-- Hence the anti-gravity set of the star library is dependency-dense. -/
theorem star_antiSet_dense (n : ℕ) :
    DepDense (starLibrary n) (antiSet (starLibrary n) n 1) := by
  apply DepDense_mono (A := ({StarThm.center} : Finset (starLibrary n).Thm))
  · intro x hx
    rw [mem_singleton] at hx
    subst hx
    exact star_center_mem_antiSet n
  · exact star_center_dense n

end AntiGravityFinite

# Computational Evidence — Anti-Gravity Mathematics

Concise numerical/structural checks performed before and during formalization.
All claims below are now backed by the sorry-free proofs in `Core.lean` and
`CatalogWitness.lean`; this file records the small-case evidence that guided them.

## 1. Small-case weight computations

Library on `Fin n`, `weight i = #{k | i ∈ deps k}`.

| Library            | n | weights (i = 0..n-1)        | ∑ weight | ∑ out-degree | match? |
|--------------------|---|-----------------------------|----------|--------------|--------|
| `discrete 4`       | 4 | 0, 0, 0, 0                  | 0        | 0            | ✓      |
| `star 4` (Fin 5)   | 5 | 4, 0, 0, 0, 0              | 4        | 4            | ✓      |
| `strongDivLibrary` | 6 | 5, 1, 2, 0, 0, 0           | 8        | 8            | ✓      |

The "∑ weight = ∑ out-degree" column is the conservation law
`total_weight_eq_total_deps`; it holds in every case computed.

For `strongDivLibrary`, deps = `![∅, {0}, {0}, {0,2}, {0,2}, {0,1}]`:
- node 0 is cited by nodes 1,2,3,4,5 → weight 5;
- node 1 is cited by node 5 → weight 1;
- node 2 is cited by nodes 3,4 → weight 2;
- nodes 3,4,5 are cited by nobody → weight 0.
Out-degrees: 0,1,1,2,2,2 → sum 8 = sum of weights. ✓

## 2. Anti-gravity density (refuting the "10%" prediction)

With threshold `(W, len) = (5, 1)`:

| Library            | #theorems | #anti-gravity | density |
|--------------------|-----------|---------------|---------|
| `discrete n`       | n         | 0             | 0       |
| `star n` (Fin n+1) | n+1       | 1 (the root)  | 1/(n+1) |
| `strongDivLibrary` | 6         | 1 (the root)  | 1/6     |

No single constant fits all three rows. The density ranges over `{0} ∪ {1/(n+1)} ∪
{1/6}`, contradicting any universal "10%" law. This is exactly what the Markov
bound `highweight_card_mul_le` predicts: density ≤ (∑ weight)/(W·n), i.e. governed
by average out-degree.

## 3. Counterexample hunt for "every library has an anti-gravity theorem"

Searched all libraries on `Fin n` with `deps ≡ ∅` (the discrete family): for every
`n`, anti-gravity count = 0 at any positive threshold. So the *universal*
existence claim ("every library contains one") is FALSE — existence is only
guaranteed when you are allowed to *choose* the library (the `star` construction),
which is what `star_root_antigravity` proves.

## 4. Sink check (no library is fully anti-gravity)

For every library on `Fin (n+1)`, the top index `Fin.last n` had weight 0 in all
computed cases (it appears in no `deps k`, since edges point backward). This
matches `top_weight_zero` and bounds anti-gravity density strictly below 1.

# Future Directions

These directions extend the finite anti-gravity calculus formalized in
`Catalog/Applications/AntiGravityFinite.lean`. Each is stated against the same
`FiniteLibrary` interface so that the existing definitions can be reused directly.

## 1. Transitive weight and a transitive pigeonhole theorem

The current `weight` counts only direct dependents, but mathematical influence
propagates along chains. The key insight is that the reflexive-transitive closure
`Relation.ReflTransGen L.depends` already present in the file lets us define a
transitive weight `twt L t := card {u | u ≠ t ∧ Relation.ReflTransGen L.depends u t}`
and ask for an analogue of `antigravity_pigeonhole` in which heaviness is
measured transitively. The subtlety is that transitive dependents are shared, so
naive summation overcounts and must be replaced by an edge-count or
path-multiplicity normalization that restores an additive budget. Why now? Because
the direct-weight pigeonhole is proved and stable, it provides an exact template
to perturb, and Mathlib's `Relation.ReflTransGen` API plus decidable finite
relations make the transitive closure computable on the finite type `Thm`.

## 2. Weight–proof-length conservation laws

The anti-gravity predicate pairs a weight lower bound with a proof-length upper
bound, but the model never forces a trade-off between the two. The key insight is
that in real libraries a theorem cannot be both arbitrarily heavy and arbitrarily
cheap once we account for the cumulative proof length along its dependency chains,
suggesting a provable conservation inequality of the form "transitive weight times
minimal chain depth is bounded below by total downstream proof cost." Formalizing
such a law would turn anti-gravity from a definition into a structural constraint
with genuine content. Why now? Because `proofLength` is already a first-class field
and the star library gives a concrete base case where the inequality can be
calibrated before attempting the general statement.

## 3. Density cores and minimal foundational sets

`DepDense` certifies that a set reaches everything, but says nothing about how
small such a set can be. The key insight is that the minimum-cardinality
dependency-dense set is exactly a minimum "foundational core" of the library, and
its size is a robust complexity invariant that `DepDense_mono` already shows is
monotone, so one can search for it via shrinking rather than growing. Developing a
Lean-verified algorithm that computes a minimal dense core (and proving its
optimality) would connect the calculus to dominating-set theory on the dependency
DAG. Why now? Because the density predicate, its monotonicity, and a worked
example (`{center}` minimal in the star library) are all in place, giving an
immediate correctness oracle for any proposed core-finding procedure.

## 4. Random and adversarial library models

The star library is a single deterministic example; the theorems hold for every
finite library but their *quantitative* force is unexplored. The key insight is
that instantiating `antigravity_pigeonhole` over a distribution of random
dependency relations turns "an anti-gravity theorem exists" into "an anti-gravity
theorem exists with high probability," yielding threshold phenomena in the
weight/budget plane analogous to random-graph thresholds. Building such models
formally would also let us study adversarial libraries engineered to *avoid*
anti-gravity and prove they must pay a measurable price in total proof length.
Why now? Because the counting theorem is fully decidable and parametric in the
relation, so a probabilistic layer can be added on top without revisiting any of
the combinatorial core.

## 5. A refactoring invariance theorem

Splitting one theorem into several lemmas is the most common library edit, and a
good importance measure should be nearly invariant under it. The key insight is
that such a split redistributes direct weight among the new lemmas while
preserving the transitive weight of the cluster, so transitive weight — not direct
weight — is the refactoring-stable invariant, and this can be stated as an
equality between transitive weights before and after an explicit graph surgery on
`FiniteLibrary`. Proving this invariance would justify promoting transitive weight
to the primary notion of anti-gravity. Why now? Because the file already separates
direct weight from the transitive-closure machinery, so the two sides of the
invariance equation can be written and compared without new infrastructure.

# A Finite Dependency Calculus for Anti-Gravity Theorems

## Abstract

We give a rigorous, fully formalized finite model of the informal *anti-gravity*
intuition for mathematical libraries: the observation that certain theorems are
simultaneously **heavy** — many other results depend directly on them — and
**cheap** — they have short proofs. Such theorems appear to "defy gravity":
despite minimal proof cost they bear a disproportionate share of the library's
downstream load. The original informal claim ("important short theorems are
dense throughout all of mathematics") is a sweeping, unfalsifiable density
statement. We replace it with a precise, provable counting theorem about *finite*
libraries, together with a reflexive-transitive density notion that we verify on
an explicit example. Every statement in this paper is mechanically checked in
Lean 4 / Mathlib in `Catalog/Applications/AntiGravityFinite.lean`, with no
`sorry`, `admit`, or vacuous placeholder, and depends only on the standard
axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, and `Quot.sound`.

## 1. The finite-library model

A library is modeled by the structure `FiniteLibrary`:

* a finite type `Thm` of theorem names (with `Fintype` and `DecidableEq`);
* a decidable **direct-dependency** relation `depends : Thm → Thm → Prop`, where
  `depends u t` means "`u` depends directly on `t`";
* a **proof-length** function `proofLength : Thm → ℕ`.

Finiteness and decidability are essential: they make the model *computational*.
Every quantity below is an honest `Finset` or `ℕ` that can in principle be
evaluated.

### Weight

The **weight** of a theorem `t` is the number of theorems that depend directly on
it:
```
weight L t := (univ.filter (fun u => L.depends u t)).card
```
Weight is the formal stand-in for "downstream importance" measured by direct use.

### The anti-gravity predicate

```
AntiGravity L K B t := K ≤ weight L t  ∧  L.proofLength t ≤ B
```
`t` is anti-gravity at thresholds `(K, B)` when it carries weight at least `K`
while costing at most `B` to prove. The two free thresholds let us speak of
"how heavy" and "how cheap" precisely, rather than vaguely.

### Derived finsets

* `shortSet L B` — the short theorems, `proofLength ≤ B`;
* `antiSet L K B` — the anti-gravity theorems at `(K, B)`;
* `totalWeightOnShort L B := ∑ t ∈ shortSet L B, weight L t` — the total direct
  weight carried by short theorems;
* `antiGravityCandidates L K B` — an executable `Finset` of candidates, proved
  (in `mem_antiGravityCandidates`) to have membership *exactly* `AntiGravity L K B t`.

## 2. Basic structural theorems

**`weight_le_card`.** For every `t`, `weight L t ≤ Fintype.card L.Thm`. Weight
cannot exceed the size of the library — the trivial but necessary boundedness
fact that anchors all counting.

**`antigravity_mono`.** If `AntiGravity L K B t`, `K' ≤ K`, and `B ≤ B'`, then
`AntiGravity L K' B' t`. Anti-gravity is monotone: weakening the weight threshold
and enlarging the proof budget only adds theorems. This is what makes the
predicate well-behaved as the thresholds vary, and underlies the density transfer
in §5.

## 3. The counting / pigeonhole theorem (replacing the speculative claim)

The informal density claim is replaced by the following honest, finite
statement and its contrapositive.

**`totalWeight_le_of_all_light` (contrapositive bound).** If every short theorem
has weight at most `K - 1`, then
```
totalWeightOnShort L B ≤ (shortSet L B).card * (K - 1).
```
This is a clean summation bound: bounding each summand by `K-1` and summing over
the short set.

**`antigravity_pigeonhole` (existence).** If `0 < K` and
```
(shortSet L B).card * (K - 1) < totalWeightOnShort L B,
```
then there exists `t` with `AntiGravity L K B t`.

In words: **if the short theorems collectively carry more direct weight than a
uniform "light" assignment could account for, then a short *heavy* theorem must
exist.** This is the precise, provable replacement for the speculative "anti-
gravity theorems are everywhere" intuition: anti-gravity is *forced* whenever
the aggregate weight on cheap theorems is large relative to the number of cheap
theorems. The proof is a genuine pigeonhole argument — assume no anti-gravity
theorem exists, deduce every short theorem is light, apply the summation bound,
and contradict the hypothesis. It is mathematically nontrivial and directly
usable: instantiating it for a concrete library produces a concrete heavy short
theorem.

## 4. Dependency density

Direct weight only sees one-step dependents. To capture global reach we use the
reflexive-transitive closure of `depends`:
```
DepDense L A := ∀ t, ∃ a, a ∈ A ∧ Relation.ReflTransGen L.depends t a.
```
`A` is **dependency-dense** when every theorem can reach some member of `A` along
chains of dependencies (allowing the empty chain). This formalizes "`A` is a
foundational core that everything ultimately rests on."

**`DepDense_mono`.** If `A ⊆ A'` and `A` is dependency-dense, so is `A'`.
Enlarging the target set preserves density — the basic monotonicity needed to
transfer density from a small explicit witness to a larger structured set.

## 5. The star library

We construct an explicit witness. The star library `starLibrary n` has theorem
names `center` and `leaf i` for `i : Fin n`; each leaf depends on `center`, and
`center` depends on nothing. We set `proofLength center = 1` and
`proofLength (leaf i) = 2`. We prove:

* **`star_weight_center`:** `weight (starLibrary n) center = n` — the center is
  depended on by exactly the `n` leaves.
* **`star_antigravity_center`:** `AntiGravity (starLibrary n) n 1 center` — the
  center is maximally heavy (`weight = n`) and maximally cheap (`proofLength = 1`).
* **`star_center_dense`:** `{center}` is dependency-dense — every theorem reaches
  the center (the center by reflexivity, each leaf by a single step).
* **`star_antiSet_dense`:** since `center ∈ antiSet (starLibrary n) n 1`, the
  singleton `{center}` is a subset of the anti-gravity set, so by
  `DepDense_mono` the **anti-gravity set itself is dependency-dense**.

The star library is the cleanest possible illustration of anti-gravity: a single
short theorem on which the entire library transitively depends, and which the
counting machinery and density machinery both certify.

## 6. From direct to transitive weight: open questions

The model measures importance by *direct* weight. The natural strengthening
replaces `weight L t` with the **transitive weight**
```
twt L t := card {u | u ≠ t ∧ Relation.ReflTransGen L.depends u t},
```
the number of theorems that depend on `t` directly *or indirectly*. Several
questions are open in this enriched model:

1. **A transitive pigeonhole.** Does an analogue of `antigravity_pigeonhole`
   hold for `twt`? The summation argument no longer applies verbatim because
   transitive dependents are heavily shared across theorems, so
   `∑_t twt L t` overcounts; the right normalization (e.g. counting *edges* of
   the transitive closure, or weighting by path multiplicity) is unclear.
2. **Weight–depth trade-offs.** Is there a provable lower bound relating
   transitive weight to proof length along dependency chains — a "conservation
   law" forcing either large `twt` or large cumulative proof cost?
3. **Density from transitive heaviness.** In the star library, transitive and
   direct weight of the center coincide. For deeper DAGs (e.g. a balanced tree),
   how does `twt` of the root grow, and when does the transitive-anti-gravity set
   remain dependency-dense?
4. **Stability under refactoring.** If a heavy theorem is split into two lemmas,
   direct weight is redistributed but transitive weight is (nearly) preserved.
   Formalizing this invariance would justify `twt` as the more robust notion of
   importance.

These extensions are stated against the same `FiniteLibrary` interface, so the
existing definitions (`DepDense`, `Relation.ReflTransGen L.depends`) already
provide the scaffolding.

## 7. Summary

We have formalized a finite dependency calculus in which the anti-gravity
intuition becomes a sequence of precise, mechanically verified theorems: weight
boundedness, monotonicity, a pigeonhole existence result with its contrapositive
counting bound, a reflexive-transitive density notion with monotonicity, and a
fully worked star-library example tying counting and density together. The
speculative "anti-gravity is dense in all of mathematics" is thereby replaced by
a rigorous statement: *in any finite library, sufficient aggregate weight on
cheap theorems forces a cheap heavy theorem to exist.*

concept.title: Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration: When Databases Form a Sheaf
concept.concept_description: Complete the proof of asymptotic corollaries of the tropical gap theorem for Markov chains. Specifically, verify that powers of row-stochastic matrices are row-stochastic (strengthening the existing incomplete proof), establish that a mixing bound implies strict positivity of the tropical cycle mean, derive a mixing speed limit from the tropical cycle mean, and prove the uniform ceiling for the tropical cycle mean when entries are bounded by 1/(n+1). All proofs must be formalized in Lean with no sorries.
concept.mathematical_framing: A database with missing entries is a partial section of a sheaf. The sheaf condition (gluing) says that if two partial sections agree on their overlap, they can be glued into a global section. Conjecture: the probability that a random database with missing rate r satisfies the sheaf condition (i.e., can be consistently filled in) is P(sheaf) = (1-r)^{C(n,k)} where n is the number of columns, k is the number of rows, and C(n,k) is the number of overlapping constraints. This means: for a database with n columns and k rows, the probability of consistent imputation drops exponentially with the number of overlapping constraints. The sheaf imputation method: fill in missing values by finding the closest global section of the data sheaf. This is equivalent to solving a constrained optimization problem where the constraints are the sheaf condition on every overlapping pair of feature subsets. Conjecture: sheaf imputation outperforms mean imputation and KNN imputation when the missing rate r < 0.5 and the number of features n > 10, because the sheaf condition provides exponentially many consistency constraints that other methods ignore. Test: generate synthetic databases with known ground truth, introduce missing values at rate r, compare sheaf imputation with mean, KNN, and MICE. Impact: data imputation is a sheaf cohomology problem. The sheaf condition is the natural consistency constraint for databases.
concept.lean_guess: Define the data sheaf: for a database with n features and m observations, the base space is the poset P of feature subsets (ordered by inclusion). The sheaf F assigns to each feature subset S the set of complete observations on features S. The restriction maps F(S) -> F(T) for T subset S project out the features in S\T. The sheaf condition: for any cover {S_i} of S, the following is an equalizer: F(S) -> prod_i F(S_i) ==> prod_{i,j} F(S_i cap S_j). This means: a global section exists iff local sections agree on overlaps. P(sheaf) = P(all overlapping constraints are consistent) = prod_{overlaps} P(consistent | missing) = prod_{overlaps} (1-r)^2 = (1-r)^{2*C(n,2)} for pairwise overlaps. More precisely: there are C(n,2) overlapping pairs of features. Each pair requires consistency of the two partial sections. P(consistent pair) = (1-r)^2 (both features present) + r^2 * P(consistent by chance) + 2*r*(1-r) * P(consistent partial). For random data: P(consistent by chance) ~ 1/k where k is the number of values. So P(sheaf) ~ (1 - r + r/k)^{C(n,2)}. For n > 10 and r < 0.5: P(sheaf) > (1-r)^{C(n,2)} > 0 if r < 1 - C(n,2)^{-1/n}. Sheaf imputation: find the global section s that minimizes ||s - data||^2 subject to s in H^0(F). This is a constrained optimization problem. Test: generate synthetic data from a known distribution, introduce MCAR missing values, compare imputation methods.

import Mathlib
import MarkovBridge.Basic

/-!
# Asymptotic Corollaries of the Tropical Gap Theorem

This file provides additional corollaries and infrastructure
for the multi-step tropical gap theorem.

## Main Results

* `pow_rowStochastic`: Powers of row-stochastic matrices are row-stochastic.
* `positive_triangleCyc_of_mixing_bound`: Existence of a mixing bound
  implies strict positivity of the tropical cycle mean.
* `mixing_speed_limit`: The tropical cycle mean imposes a speed limit
  on mixing — transition probabilities cannot decay faster than
  `exp(-m · triangleCyc)`.
* `uniform_ceiling_from_entry_bound`: When ALL single-step entries
  satisfy `P i j ≤ 1/(n+1)`, the tropical cycle mean is at least `log(n+1)`.

## Note on the asymptotic ceiling

The statement `log(n+1) ≤ triangleCyc(-log P)` does NOT hold for
arbitrary positive row-stochastic matrices with uniform mixing convergence.
Counterexample: `P = [[0.99, 0.01], [0.01, 0.99]]` on 2 states has
`triangleCyc ≈ -log(0.99) ≈ 0.01 < log(2) ≈ 0.69`.
The theorem DOES hold when single-step entries are already bounded by `1/(n+1)`.
-/

noncomputable section

open Finset BigOperators Real Matrix Filter

namespace MarkovTropicalBridge

variable {n : ℕ}

/-! ## Row-stochastic powers -/

/-
Row-stochastic matrices have power entries bounded above by 1.
-/
lemma pow_entry_le_one
    (P : Matrix (Fin (n+1)) (Fin (n+1)) ℝ)
    (hrow : RowStochastic P) (m : ℕ) (i j : Fin (n+1)) :
    (P ^ m) i j ≤ 1 := by
  -- By induction on $m$, we can show that the sum of the entries in each row of $P^m$ is 1.
  have h_row_sum : ∀ m i, ∑ j, (P ^ m) i j = 1 := by
    intro m i; induction' m with m ih generalizing i <;> simp_all +decide [ pow_succ', Matrix.mul_apply, Finset.mul_sum _ _ _ ] ;
    · simp +decide [ Matrix.one_apply ];
    · rw [ Finset.sum_comm ];
      simp +decide [ ← Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, ← Finset.sum_mul, hrow.2, ih ];
  exact h_row_sum m i ▸ Finset.single_le_sum ( fun a _ => show 0 ≤ ( P ^ m ) i a from by
                                                            apply MarkovTropicalBridge.pow_entry_nonneg <;> simp_all +decide [ pow_succ, Matrix.mul_apply ];
                                                            exact hrow.1 ) ( Finset.mem_univ j )

/-
Row sums are preserved under matrix powers.
-/
lemma pow_row_sum_eq_one
    (P : Matrix (Fin (n+1)) (Fin (n+1)) ℝ)
    (hrow : RowStochastic P) (m : ℕ) (i : Fin (n+1)) :
    ∑ j, (P ^ m) i j = 1 := by
  have h_sum_transpose : ∀ m : ℕ, ∀ i : Fin (n + 1), ∑ j, (P ^ m) i j = 1 := by
    intro m i; induction' m with m ih generalizing i <;> simp_all +decide [ pow_succ', Matrix.mul_apply, Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, Finset.sum_mul ] ;
    · simp +decide [ Matrix.one_apply ];
    · rw [ Finset.sum_comm ];
      simp +decide [ ← Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, ← Finset.sum_mul, hrow.2, ih ];
  convert h_sum_transpose m i using 1

/-- Powers of row-stochastic matrices are row-stochastic. -/
lemma pow_rowStochastic
    (P : Matrix (Fin (n+1)) (Fin (n+1)) ℝ)
    (hrow : RowStochastic P) (m : ℕ) :
    RowStochastic (P ^ m) :=
  ⟨fun i j => pow_entry_nonneg hrow.1 m i j, pow_row_sum_eq_one P hrow m⟩

/-! ## Positivity of tropical cycle mean -/

/-
**Positivity from mixing.**
If there exist `m ≥ 1` and `α < 1` such that all `m`-step transition
probabilities are at most `α`, then the tropical cycle mean is
strictly positive.
-/
theorem positive_triangleCyc_of_mixing_bound
    (P : Matrix (Fin (n+1)) (Fin (n+1)) ℝ)
    (hrow : RowStochastic P) (hpos : PositiveMatrix P)
    {m : ℕ} (hm : 1 ≤ m) {α : ℝ} (hα : 0 < α) (hα1 : α < 1)
    (hpow : ∀ i j, (P ^ m) i j ≤ α) :
    0 < triangleCyc (tropicalCost P) := by
  exact lt_of_lt_of_le ( by exact div_pos ( neg_pos_of_neg ( Real.log_neg hα hα1 ) ) ( by positivity ) ) ( multi_step_tropical_gap P hrow hpos α hα hα1 hm hpow )

/-! ## Mixing speed limit -/

/-
**Mixing speed limit.**
The tropical cycle mean sets a lower bound on how quickly transition
probabilities can decay. For any `m ≥ 1`, the best achievable uniform
mixing bound `α` satisfies `α ≥ exp(-m · triangleCyc(-log P))`.

Equivalently: `-log α ≤ m · triangleCyc(-log P)`.

This is just `multi_step_tropical_gap_mul` rephrased.
-/

    (h₁ : spDist N₁ ≤ spDist N₁') (h₂ : spDist N₂ ≤ spDist N₂') :
    spDist (.series N₁ N₂) ≤ spDist (.series N₁' N₂') := by
  simp [spDist]; linarith

/-- Parallel composition is monotone in both arguments. -/
theorem parallel_mono {N₁ N₁' N₂ N₂' : SPNet}
    (h₁ : spDist N₁ ≤ spDist N₁') (h₂ : spDist N₂ ≤ spDist N₂') :
    spDist (.parallel N₁ N₂) ≤ spDist (.parallel N₁' N₂') := by
  simp only [spDist]; exact min_le_min h₁ h₂

/-! ## Lipschitz property of series composition -/

/-- Series composition is 1-Lipschitz in each argument (fixing the other). -/
theorem series_lipschitz_left (N₂ : SPNet) (N₁ N₁' : SPNet) :
    |spDist (.series N₁ N₂) - spDist (.series N₁' N₂)| =
    |spDist N₁ - spDist N₁'| := by
  simp only [spDist]; ring_nf

/-! ## Hyperbolicity connection -/

/-- For any SP network, the four-point condition on {source, sink} is
    trivially satisfied since two-point spaces are 0-hyperbolic. -/
theorem sp_pair_zero_hyperbolic (N : SPNet) :
    ∀ w x y z : Fin 2,
      let d : Fin 2 → Fin 2 → ℝ := fun i j =>
        if i = j then 0 else spDist N
      d w x + d y z ≤
        max (d w y + d x z) (d w z + d x y) + 2 * 0 :=
  sp_two_terminal_zero_hyperbolic N

/-! ## Tropical matrix encoding of SP networks -/

/-- Encode a two-terminal SP network as a 2×2 tropical matrix. -/
noncomputable def spToMatrix (N : SPNet) : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℝ :=
  fun i j => if i = j then 0 else spDist N

/-- The matrix encoding preserves the boundary distance. -/
theorem spToMatrix_encodes (N : SPNet) :
    spToMatrix N 0 1 = spDist N := by
  simp [spToMatrix]

/-- SP-equivalent networks produce the same matrix. -/
theorem spToMatrix_equiv (N₁ N₂ : SPNet) (h : SPEquiv N₁ N₂) :
    spToMatrix N₁ = spToMatrix N₂ := by
  ext i j
  simp only [spToMatrix]
  split <;> simp_all [SPEquiv]

/-
The tropical matrix product of two SP encoding matrices at (0,1) equals
    the minimum of the two boundary distances (= parallel composition distance).
    This is because the 2×2 tropical product computes min over intermediate vertices:
    min(0 + d(N₂), d(N₁) + 0) = min(d(N₁), d(N₂)).
-/
theorem spMatrix_product_eq_parallel (N₁ N₂ : SPNet) :
    tropicalMatMul (spToMatrix N₁) (spToMatrix N₂) 0 1 =
    spDist (.parallel N₁ N₂) := by
  -- Apply the definition of tropical matrix multiplication.
  unfold tropicalMatMul spToMatrix;
  rw [ @ciInf_eq_of_forall_ge_of_forall_gt_exists_lt ];
  · simp +decide [ Fin.forall_fin_two, spDist_parallel ];
  · intro w hw;
    contrapose! hw;
    exact le_min ( by simpa using hw 1 ) ( by simpa using hw 0 )

/-! ## Summary: The three-way bridge -/

/-- **Summary theorem**: For series-parallel networks:
    1. Boundary distance = tropical expression evaluation (algebraic structure)
    2. Boundary distance is a complete invariant for SP-equivalence (rigidity)
    3. The boundary metric satisfies the four-point condition (hyperbolicity)
    4. The boundary data can be encoded as tropical matrix operations

    This theorem packages all four facts. -/
theorem sp_three_way_bridge (N : SPNet) :
    -- 1. Tropical expression evaluation equals boundary distance
    (spToExpr N).eval = spDist N ∧
    -- 2. SP-equivalence ↔ equal boundary distance
    (∀ N', SPEquiv N N' ↔ spDist N = spDist N') ∧
    -- 3. Boundary distance is positive
    0 < spDist N ∧
    -- 4. Matrix encoding preserves distance
    spToMatrix N 0 1 = spDist N := by
  refine ⟨sp_eval_eq_dist N, fun N' => Iff.rfl, spDist_pos N, spToMatrix_encodes N⟩

end TropicalBridge

# Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration — Core

This file develops, self-containedly, the theory of the **data sheaf** of a
database with missing entries, on the poset of finite sets of rows.  It is the
foundational module of the `Applications.SheafDataIntegration` cluster.

It re-derives the basic presheaf/sheaf structure (restriction maps,
functoriality, locality and gluing) and adds the headline structural result:

* `dataSheaf_glue_unique` — the data presheaf is a **sheaf**: a compatible
  family of local sections over a cover glues to a *unique* global section
  (existence + uniqueness packaged as `∃!`).  This is the precise sense in
  which "databases form a sheaf".

It also records that the data sheaf is always non-empty when the value type is
inhabited (`dataSection_nonempty`): every database admits at least one
consistent completion (e.g. default imputation).

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis: the separation (locality) and gluing axioms can be combined into
-- a single equalizer/`∃!` statement, which is the cleanest formulation of
-- "databases form a sheaf".  Experiment: state `dataSheaf_glue_unique` and
-- derive it from `DataSheaf.gluing` (existence) and `DataSheaf.locality`
-- (uniqueness).  Outcome: succeeds; the proof is a short combination.
-- Insight: the row-poset `Finset (Fin k)` carries the trivial Grothendieck
-- topology where covers are arbitrary inclusions, and the data presheaf is a
-- sheaf for it because sections are determined cell-by-cell.
-/

import Mathlib

noncomputable section

open Finset Function

namespace SheafDataIntegration

/-! ## §1. Databases and partial sections -/

/-- A **database** with `n` columns and `k` rows, where each cell is either an
observed value `some a` or a missing value `none`. -/
structure Database (α : Type*) (n k : ℕ) where
  /-- `entry i j` is the content of row `i`, column `j`. -/
  entry : Fin k → Fin n → Option α

variable {α : Type*} {n k : ℕ}

/-- The set of **observed** (non-missing) cells of a database. -/
def Database.observed (D : Database α n k) : Set (Fin k × Fin n) :=
  {p | (D.entry p.1 p.2).isSome}

/-- The **partial section** of a database: the function defined on the observed
(non-missing) cells returning the observed value. -/
def Database.partialSection (D : Database α n k) :
    ∀ p : Fin k × Fin n, (D.entry p.1 p.2).isSome → α :=
  fun p h => (D.entry p.1 p.2).get h

/-! ## §2. The data sheaf and its sheaf axioms -/

/-- A **section** of the data sheaf over a finite set of rows `R`: a total
assignment of a value in `α` to every cell of every row in `R`, agreeing with
the observed values of the database (extending the partial section). -/
abbrev DataSection (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) : Type _ :=
  { g : R → Fin n → α //
      ∀ (i : R) (j : Fin n) (h : (D.entry (i : Fin k) j).isSome),
        (D.entry (i : Fin k) j).get h = g i j }

/-- The **restriction map** of the data presheaf, from a section over `R` to a
section over a smaller row set `R' ⊆ R`. -/
def restrictSec (D : Database α n k) {R R' : Finset (Fin k)} (h : R' ⊆ R)
    (s : DataSection D R) : DataSection D R' :=
  ⟨fun i => s.1 ⟨(i : Fin k), h i.2⟩,
   fun i j hj => s.2 ⟨(i : Fin k), h i.2⟩ j hj⟩

/-- **Identity axiom**: restricting along the identity inclusion does nothing. -/
theorem restrictSec_self (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k))
    (s : DataSection D R) : restrictSec D (le_refl R) s = s := by
  convert rfl

/-- **Functoriality**: restriction is compatible with composition of inclusions. -/
theorem restrictSec_comp (D : Database α n k) {R R' R'' : Finset (Fin k)}
    (h1 : R'' ⊆ R') (h2 : R' ⊆ R) (s : DataSection D R) :
    restrictSec D h1 (restrictSec D h2 s) = restrictSec D (h1.trans h2) s := by
  rfl

/-- **Locality / separation axiom**: if two global sections over `R` restrict to
equal sections on every member of a cover of `R`, then they are equal. -/
theorem DataSheaf.locality (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) {ι : Type*}
    (cover : ι → Finset (Fin k)) (hsub : ∀ a, cover a ⊆ R)
    (hcov : ∀ i ∈ R, ∃ a, i ∈ cover a) (s t : DataSection D R)
    (h : ∀ a, restrictSec D (hsub a) s = restrictSec D (hsub a) t) : s = t := by
  refine Subtype.ext (funext fun i => ?_)
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hcov i i.2
  convert congr_arg Subtype.val (h a) |> congr_arg (fun f => f ⟨i, ha⟩) using 1

/-- **Gluing axiom**: a compatible family of local sections over a cover of `R`
glues to a (global) section over `R` restricting to each. -/
theorem DataSheaf.gluing (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) {ι : Type*}
    (cover : ι → Finset (Fin k)) (hsub : ∀ a, cover a ⊆ R)
    (hcov : ∀ i ∈ R, ∃ a, i ∈ cover a) (s : ∀ a, DataSection D (cover a))
    (hcompat : ∀ (a b : ι) (i : Fin k) (hia : i ∈ cover a) (hib : i ∈ cover b),
        (s a).1 ⟨i, hia⟩ = (s b).1 ⟨i, hib⟩) :
    ∃ g : DataSection D R, ∀ a, restrictSec D (hsub a) g = s a := by
  refine ⟨⟨fun i => (s (Classical.choose (hcov i i.2)) |> Subtype.val)
      ⟨i, Classical.choose_spec (hcov i i.2)⟩, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
  · exact fun i j hj => (s (Classical.choose (hcov i i.2))).2
      ⟨i, Classical.choose_spec (hcov i i.2)⟩ j hj ▸ rfl
  · intro a; ext i
    exact hcompat _ _ _ (Classical.choose_spec (hcov _ (hsub _ i.2))) i.2 ▸ rfl

/-! ## §3. Databases form a sheaf: unique gluing (equalizer) -/

/-
**Databases form a sheaf.** A compatible family of local sections over a
cover of the row set `R` glues to a *unique* global section restricting to each
member of the family.  This packages the separation axiom
(`DataSheaf.locality`, uniqueness) and the gluing axiom (`DataSheaf.gluing`,
existence) into a single equalizer/`∃!` statement — the precise sense in which
"databases form a sheaf".
-/
theorem dataSheaf_glue_unique (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) {ι : Type*}
    (cover : ι → Finset (Fin k)) (hsub : ∀ a, cover a ⊆ R)
    (hcov : ∀ i ∈ R, ∃ a, i ∈ cover a) (s : ∀ a, DataSection D (cover a))
    (hcompat : ∀ (a b : ι) (i : Fin k) (hia : i ∈ cover a) (hib : i ∈ cover b),
        (s a).1 ⟨i, hia⟩ = (s b).1 ⟨i, hib⟩) :
    ∃! g : DataSection D R, ∀ a, restrictSec D (hsub a) g = s a := by
  obtain ⟨ g, hg ⟩ := DataSheaf.gluing D R cover hsub hcov s hcompat;
  refine' ⟨ g, hg, fun g' hg' => _ ⟩;
  exact DataSheaf.locality D R cover hsub hcov g' g fun a => hg' a ▸ hg a ▸ rfl

/-! ## §4. Non-emptiness: every database has a consistent completion -/

/-
**Existence of a consistent completion.** When the value type is inhabited,
the data sheaf over any row set is non-empty: every database admits at least
one total assignment extending its observed cells (e.g. default imputation of
missing cells).
-/
theorem dataSection_nonempty [Inhabited α] (D : Database α n k)
    (R : Finset (Fin k)) : Nonempty (DataSection D R) := by
  refine' ⟨ ⟨ fun i j => if h : ( D.entry i j ).isSome then ( D.entry i j ).get h else default, _ ⟩ ⟩;
  grind

end SheafDataIntegration

# Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration — Counting consistent completions

This module counts the **global sections** of the data sheaf: the consistent
completions of a database over a set of rows.  The headline result is the exact
formula

  `#(consistent completions) = qᵐ`,

where `q = #α` is the number of possible cell values and `m` is the number of
*missing* cells in the chosen rows.  This is the structural / enumerative
counterpart of the probabilistic `q ^ C` law: each missing cell contributes one
independent degree of freedom.

## Main results

* `dataSection_equivFree` — a consistent completion is the same data as a free
  choice of value for each missing cell (`DataSection D R ≃ (FreeCell D R → α)`).
* `card_dataSection` — `#(DataSection D R) = (#α) ^ #(FreeCell D R)`.
* `freeCell_card_eq_missingCells` — the number of free cells equals the
  combinatorial count `missingCells`.
* `card_dataSection_eq` — `#(DataSection D R) = (#α) ^ missingCells D R`.
* `card_dataSection_pos` — there is always at least one consistent completion.
* `unique_completion_of_fullyObserved` — a fully-observed database has a unique
  completion.
* `nonunique_completion_of_missing` — with ≥ 2 possible values, a missing cell
  forces at least two distinct completions.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis: the "missing data = degrees of freedom" intuition can be made
-- exact: completions are in bijection with arbitrary value-assignments to the
-- missing cells, the observed cells being pinned.  Experiment: build the Equiv
-- `DataSection D R ≃ (FreeCell D R → α)` explicitly (observed cells forced to
-- `Option.get`, free cells arbitrary) and read off the cardinality via
-- `Fintype.card_fun`.  Outcome: the bijection is clean; cardinality is a one-
-- liner once the equiv is in hand.
-- Insight: this gives a *sheaf-theoretic derivation* of the `q ^ C` decay law —
-- the exponent is literally the number of sheaf degrees of freedom, and it is
-- additive over rows (`missingCells` is a sum over rows), mirroring the
-- independence used in the probabilistic computation.
-- Failure analysis: an earlier attempt indexed free cells by `Fin k × Fin n`
-- with a membership side-condition; switching to the subtype of `↥R × Fin n`
-- made the `Fintype` instance and the sum decomposition straightforward.
-/

import Mathlib
import Applications.SheafDataIntegration.Core

noncomputable section

open Finset Function

namespace SheafDataIntegration

variable {α : Type*} {n k : ℕ}

/-! ## §1. Free cells (the missing cells, indexed as a subtype) -/

/-- A **free cell** of a database over a set of rows `R`: a pair `(i, j)` with
`i ∈ R` (as an element of the coercion `↥R`) whose entry is *missing*.  These
are exactly the cells whose value a completion is free to choose. -/
abbrev FreeCell (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) : Type _ :=
  { p : R × Fin n // D.entry (p.1 : Fin k) p.2 = none }

/-- The number of missing cells among the rows of `R`, as a sum over rows. -/
def missingCells (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) : ℕ :=
  ∑ i ∈ R, (Finset.univ.filter (fun j : Fin n => D.entry i j = none)).card

/-! ## §2. Completions are free choices on the missing cells -/

/-- Read off the values of a completion at the (free) missing cells. -/
def toFreeFun (D : Database α n k) {R : Finset (Fin k)}
    (s : DataSection D R) : FreeCell D R → α :=
  fun p => s.1 p.1.1 p.1.2

/-- Reconstruct a completion from a free choice on the missing cells: observed
cells take their recorded value, missing cells take the chosen value. -/
def ofFreeFun (D : Database α n k) {R : Finset (Fin k)}
    (f : FreeCell D R → α) : DataSection D R :=
  ⟨fun i j => if h : (D.entry (i : Fin k) j).isSome then (D.entry (i : Fin k) j).get h
      else f ⟨(i, j), Option.not_isSome_iff_eq_none.mp h⟩,
   by
     intro i j h
     dsimp only
     rw [dif_pos h]⟩

@[simp] theorem toFreeFun_ofFreeFun (D : Database α n k) {R : Finset (Fin k)}
    (f : FreeCell D R → α) : toFreeFun D (ofFreeFun D f) = f := by
  ext ⟨ ⟨ i, j ⟩, h ⟩ ; simp +decide [ *, toFreeFun, ofFreeFun ] ;

@[simp] theorem ofFreeFun_toFreeFun (D : Database α n k) {R : Finset (Fin k)}
    (s : DataSection D R) : ofFreeFun D (toFreeFun D s) = s := by
  ext ⟨ i, hi ⟩ j ; unfold ofFreeFun ; unfold toFreeFun ; aesop

/-- **Completions = free choices on missing cells.** A consistent completion of
`D` over `R` is exactly a free assignment of a value to each missing cell, the
observed cells being forced to their recorded value. -/
def dataSection_equivFree (D : Database α n k)
    (R : Finset (Fin k)) : DataSection D R ≃ (FreeCell D R → α) where
  toFun := toFreeFun D
  invFun := ofFreeFun D
  left_inv := ofFreeFun_toFreeFun D
  right_inv := toFreeFun_ofFreeFun D

/-! ## §3. The counting formula -/

/-
**Counting (raw form).** The number of consistent completions equals the
number of possible cell values raised to the number of free (missing) cells.
-/
theorem card_dataSection [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α] (D : Database α n k)
    (R : Finset (Fin k)) :
    Fintype.card (DataSection D R) = (Fintype.card α) ^ (Fintype.card (FreeCell D R)) := by
  rw [ ← Fintype.card_fun, Fintype.card_congr ( dataSection_equivFree D R ) ]

/-
The number of free cells equals the combinatorial `missingCells` count.
-/
theorem freeCell_card_eq_missingCells [DecidableEq α] (D : Database α n k)
    (R : Finset (Fin k)) :
    Fintype.card (FreeCell D R) = missingCells D R := by
  rw [ Fintype.card_subtype ];
  rw [ Finset.card_filter ];
  convert Finset.sum_product ( Finset.univ : Finset R ) ( Finset.univ : Finset ( Fin n ) ) _ using 1;
  refine' Finset.sum_bij ( fun x hx => ⟨ x, hx ⟩ ) _ _ _ _ <;> simp +decide

/-- **Counting (closed form).** `#(consistent completions) = (#α) ^ (missing cells)`. -/
theorem card_dataSection_eq [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α] (D : Database α n k)
    (R : Finset (Fin k)) :
    Fintype.card (DataSection D R) = (Fintype.card α) ^ missingCells D R := by
  rw [card_dataSection, freeCell_card_eq_missingCells]

/-! ## §4. Consequences -/

/-
**Existence (finite form).** There is always at least one consistent
completion (when there is at least one possible value).
-/
theorem card_dataSection_pos [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α] [Nonempty α]
    (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) :
    0 < Fintype.card (DataSection D R) := by
  -- By `card_dataSection_eq`, the count is `(Fintype.card α) ^ missingCells D R`.
  rw [card_dataSection_eq];
  exact pow_pos ( Fintype.card_pos ) _

/-- **Uniqueness for fully-observed data.** If no cell is missing, the database
has exactly one consistent completion (itself). -/
theorem unique_completion_of_fullyObserved [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α]
    (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) (h : missingCells D R = 0) :
    Fintype.card (DataSection D R) = 1 := by
  rw [card_dataSection_eq, h, pow_zero]

/-
**Non-uniqueness from missing data.** If there are at least two possible
values and at least one missing cell, there are at least two distinct
consistent completions.
-/
theorem nonunique_completion_of_missing [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α]
    (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k))
    (hα : 2 ≤ Fintype.card α) (hmiss : 1 ≤ missingCells D R) :
    2 ≤ Fintype.card (DataSection D R) := by
  convert Nat.pow_le_pow_left hα 1 |> le_trans <| Nat.pow_le_pow_right ( by linarith ) hmiss using 1;
  convert card_dataSection_eq D R

/-! ## §5. Independence across disjoint blocks of rows -/

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis: the `q ^ missing` law makes "rows are independent degrees of
-- freedom" precise: over disjoint row sets the missing counts add, hence the
-- completion counts multiply.  This is the enumerative analogue of the
-- probabilistic independence used to derive the `q ^ C` consistency law.

/-- The missing count is additive over disjoint blocks of rows. -/
theorem missingCells_union_disjoint (D : Database α n k) {R₁ R₂ : Finset (Fin k)}
    (h : Disjoint R₁ R₂) :
    missingCells D (R₁ ∪ R₂) = missingCells D R₁ + missingCells D R₂ := by
  unfold missingCells
  rw [Finset.sum_union h]

/-- **Independence across disjoint row blocks.** The number of consistent
completions over a disjoint union of row sets is the product of the counts over
each block — the enumerative shadow of probabilistic independence. -/
theorem card_dataSection_union_disjoint [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α]
    (D : Database α n k) {R₁ R₂ : Finset (Fin k)} (h : Disjoint R₁ R₂) :
    Fintype.card (DataSection D (R₁ ∪ R₂)) =
      Fintype.card (DataSection D R₁) * Fintype.card (DataSection D R₂) := by
  rw [card_dataSection_eq, card_dataSection_eq, card_dataSection_eq,
    missingCells_union_disjoint D h, pow_add]

end SheafDataIntegration

# Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration — Merging databases

This module formalizes **data integration** itself: combining two databases
over the same schema into one.  The merge `D₁ ⊔ D₂` keeps every observed cell of
either source (preferring `D₁` on overlaps).  The central theorem says that,
*when the two sources agree on their common observed cells*, the consistent
completions of the merge are exactly the assignments consistent with **both**
sources simultaneously:

  `Consistent (merge D₁ D₂) R g ↔ Consistent D₁ R g ∧ Consistent D₂ R g`.

This is the sheaf-theoretic content of integration: gluing data sources
intersects their section spaces.  Quantitatively, integration can only *remove*
degrees of freedom, so it never increases the number of consistent completions.

## Main results

* `Database.merge` — the integrated database (observed cells of either source).
* `merge_observed_eq` — `observed (merge D₁ D₂) = observed D₁ ∪ observed D₂`.
* `consistent_merge_iff` — completions of the merge = completions of both
  sources (under agreement on overlaps).
* `missingCells_merge_le_left` / `_right` — merging never increases the missing
  count.
* `card_dataSection_merge_le_left` — integration never increases the number of
  consistent completions.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-- Hypothesis: "integrating datasets" = "gluing sections", and the resulting
-- section space is the *intersection* (equalizer/pullback) of the two source
-- section spaces, exactly when the sources are compatible on overlaps.
-- Experiment: define the merge by `Option`-preference and prove
-- `consistent_merge_iff`.  Outcome: the forward direction needs the agreement
-- hypothesis (an overlap where D₁ and D₂ disagree would over-constrain), while
-- the backward direction is unconditional.
-- Insight: combined with the counting law `#completions = q^(missing)`, the
-- iff yields a *monotonicity* principle for data integration — adding a
-- consistent source can only shrink (never grow) the completion space, since it
-- can only reveal (never hide) cells.  This is the enumerative shadow of the
-- equalizer description of a sheaf.
-- Failure analysis: stating the merge via `Option.orElse`/`<|>` made the
-- case-split lemmas awkward; an explicit `match` on `D₁.entry i j` keeps the
-- `get`/`isSome` reasoning transparent.
-/

import Mathlib
import Applications.SheafDataIntegration.Core
import Applications.SheafDataIntegration.Counting

noncomputable section

open Finset Function

namespace SheafDataIntegration

variable {α : Type*} {n k : ℕ}

/-! ## §1. The merge of two databases -/

/-- The **merge** (integration) of two databases over the same schema: each cell
is the observed value of `D₁` if present, otherwise that of `D₂`. -/
def Database.merge (D₁ D₂ : Database α n k) : Database α n k where
  entry i j := match D₁.entry i j with
    | some a => some a
    | none => D₂.entry i j

/-- The consistency predicate underlying `DataSection`: `g` agrees with every
observed cell of `D`.  By definition `DataSection D R = { g // Consistent D R g }`. -/
def Consistent (D : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) (g : R → Fin n → α) : Prop :=
  ∀ (i : R) (j : Fin n) (h : (D.entry (i : Fin k) j).isSome),
    (D.entry (i : Fin k) j).get h = g i j

/-! ## §2. Observed cells of a merge -/

/-
The observed cells of a merge are the union of the observed cells of the
sources.
-/
theorem merge_observed_eq (D₁ D₂ : Database α n k) :
    (Database.merge D₁ D₂).observed = D₁.observed ∪ D₂.observed := by
  ext p;
  cases h : D₁.entry p.1 p.2 <;> simp +decide [ *, Database.merge, Database.observed ]

/-! ## §3. Integration = intersection of section spaces -/

/-
**Integration theorem.** If `D₁` and `D₂` agree on every cell they both
observe, then an assignment `g` is consistent with the merge if and only if it
is consistent with each source.  Thus integrating two compatible data sources
*intersects* their spaces of consistent completions.
-/
theorem consistent_merge_iff (D₁ D₂ : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k))
    (agree : ∀ (i : Fin k) (j : Fin n) (a b : α),
      D₁.entry i j = some a → D₂.entry i j = some b → a = b)
    (g : R → Fin n → α) :
    Consistent (Database.merge D₁ D₂) R g ↔ Consistent D₁ R g ∧ Consistent D₂ R g := by
  constructor <;> intro h;
  · constructor;
    · intro i j h₁;
      convert h i j _ using 1;
      unfold Database.merge;
      grind;
      unfold Database.merge; aesop;
    · intro i j h₂;
      specialize h i j;
      cases h₁ : D₁.entry i j <;> simp_all +decide [ Database.merge ];
      specialize agree i j ( g i j ) ( ( D₂.entry i j ).get h₂ ) h₁ ; aesop;
  · intro i j h';
    grind +locals

/-! ## §4. Integration never increases the completion count -/

/-
Merging can only reveal cells, so the missing count does not increase
(relative to the first source).
-/
theorem missingCells_merge_le_left (D₁ D₂ : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) :
    missingCells (Database.merge D₁ D₂) R ≤ missingCells D₁ R := by
  refine' Finset.sum_le_sum fun i hi => Finset.card_le_card _;
  intro j hj; unfold Database.merge at hj; aesop;

/-
Merging can only reveal cells, so the missing count does not increase
(relative to the second source).
-/
theorem missingCells_merge_le_right (D₁ D₂ : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) :
    missingCells (Database.merge D₁ D₂) R ≤ missingCells D₂ R := by
  refine' Finset.sum_le_sum fun i hi => _;
  refine' Finset.card_mono _;
  intro j hj; simp_all +decide [ Database.merge ] ;
  cases h : D₁.entry i j <;> aesop

/-
**Monotonicity of integration.** Integrating an extra source never increases
the number of consistent completions.
-/
theorem card_dataSection_merge_le_left [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α] [Nonempty α]
    (D₁ D₂ : Database α n k) (R : Finset (Fin k)) :
    Fintype.card (DataSection (Database.merge D₁ D₂) R) ≤
      Fintype.card (DataSection D₁ R) := by
  have := @missingCells_merge_le_left;
  exact ( this D₁ D₂ R ) |> fun h => by rw [SheafDataIntegration.card_dataSection_eq, SheafDataIntegration.card_dataSection_eq]; exact Nat.pow_le_pow_right (by positivity) h;

end SheafDataIntegration

  fun ⟨i, j⟩ => if j.val = 3 ∧ (i.val = 2 ∨ i.val = 3 ∨ i.val = 4) then 1 else 0

    tropicalLifeStep (by omega : 0 < 8) (by omega : 0 < 8) blinkerH8 = blinkerV8 := by

/-- The vertical blinker evolves back to the horizontal blinker in one step. -/

    tropicalLifeStep (by omega : 0 < 8) (by omega : 0 < 8) blinkerV8 = blinkerH8 := by
  native_decide

theorem blinker_period_2 :

  simp [Function.iterate_succ, Function.comp, blinker_step_HV, blinker_step_VH]

/-! ## Local Stability Characterization -/

/-- A cell is locally stable if the local rule fixes it. -/
def locallyStable {m n : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m) (hn : 0 < n) (c : Config m n)
    (x : Cell m n) : Prop :=
  tropicalLocalRule hm hn c x = c x

/-- A configuration is a still life if and only if every cell is locally stable.

theorem still_life_iff_all_locally_stable {m n : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m) (hn : 0 < n)
    (c : Config m n) :
    IsStillLife hm hn c ↔ ∀ x, locallyStable hm hn c x := by
  simp only [IsStillLife, tropicalLifeStep, funext_iff, locallyStable]

  - `FiniteStatModel`: A parametric family of probability distributions on a finite sample space
  - `scoreVec`: The score vector (gradient of log-likelihood)
  - `fisherMatrix`: The Fisher information matrix

import Mathlib

/-! ## Core Statistical Model -/

/-- A finite parametric statistical model: a family of probability mass functions
    indexed by a parameter `θ ∈ Θ`, over a finite sample space `Ω`. -/
structure FiniteStatModel (Θ Ω : Type*) [Fintype Ω] where
  /-- The log-likelihood function -/
  logLik    : Θ → Ω → ℝ
  /-- The probability mass function -/
  pmf       : Θ → Ω → ℝ
  /-- Probabilities are nonneg -/
  pmf_nonneg : ∀ θ ω, 0 ≤ pmf θ ω
  /-- Probabilities sum to 1 -/
  pmf_sum_one : ∀ θ, ∑ ω : Ω, pmf θ ω = 1
  /-- Log-likelihood is consistent with pmf where pmf is nonzero -/
  logLik_spec : ∀ θ ω, pmf θ ω ≠ 0 → logLik θ ω = Real.log (pmf θ ω)

variable {n : ℕ} {Ω : Type*} [Fintype Ω] [DecidableEq Ω]

/-! ## Score and Fisher Information -/

/-- The Fisher information matrix: I_{ij}(θ) = 𝔼_θ[sᵢ(θ,X) sⱼ(θ,X)]
    = ∑_ω p(ω;θ) sᵢ(θ,ω) sⱼ(θ,ω).
    Here `dlogp` represents the score function (partial derivatives of log p). -/
def fisherMatrix (M : FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω)
    (dlogp : (Fin n → ℝ) → Ω → Fin n → ℝ) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ :=
  Matrix.of fun i j => ∑ ω : Ω, M.pmf θ ω * dlogp θ ω i * dlogp θ ω j

/-! ## Expectation, Variance, Covariance -/

/-- Expectation of a real-valued function under the model at parameter θ. -/
def expectationAt {Θ : Type*} (M : FiniteStatModel Θ Ω) (θ : Θ) (f : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ ω : Ω, M.pmf θ ω * f ω

/-- Variance of a real-valued function under the model at parameter θ. -/
def varianceAt {Θ : Type*} (M : FiniteStatModel Θ Ω) (θ : Θ) (f : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  expectationAt M θ (fun ω => (f ω - expectationAt M θ f) ^ 2)

/-- Covariance of two real-valued functions under the model at parameter θ. -/
def covarianceAt {Θ : Type*} (M : FiniteStatModel Θ Ω) (θ : Θ) (f g : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  expectationAt M θ (fun ω => (f ω - expectationAt M θ f) * (g ω - expectationAt M θ g))

/-! ## Regularity and Unbiasedness -/

/-- Regularity hypotheses for a finite statistical model with score function. -/
structure RegularityHypotheses (M : FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω)
    (dlogp : (Fin n → ℝ) → Ω → Fin n → ℝ) : Prop where
  /-- All probabilities are strictly positive -/
  pmf_pos : ∀ θ ω, 0 < M.pmf θ ω
  /-- The score has mean zero: ∑_ω p(ω;θ) sᵢ(θ,ω) = 0 for all i. -/
  score_mean_zero : ∀ θ (i : Fin n), ∑ ω : Ω, M.pmf θ ω * dlogp θ ω i = 0

/-- Directional derivative of g at θ in direction v, defined via Fréchet derivative. -/
def directionalDeriv (g : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ) (θ v : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (fderiv ℝ g θ) v

/-! ## Exponential Families -/

/-- An exponential family on a finite sample space: p_θ(ω) = exp(⟨θ, T(ω)⟩ - ψ(θ) + k(ω))
    where T is the sufficient statistic, ψ is the log-partition function, and k is the
    base measure log-density. -/
structure ExponentialFamily (n : ℕ) (Ω : Type*) [Fintype Ω] where
  /-- Sufficient statistic T : Ω → ℝⁿ -/
  suffStat : Ω → Fin n → ℝ
  /-- Base measure log-density k : Ω → ℝ -/
  baseMeasure : Ω → ℝ
  /-- Normalizing condition: the partition function is finite and positive -/
  partition_pos : ∀ θ : Fin n → ℝ,
    0 < ∑ ω : Ω, Real.exp (∑ i, θ i * suffStat ω i + baseMeasure ω)

/-- The log-partition (cumulant generating) function ψ(θ) = log ∑_ω exp(⟨θ,T(ω)⟩ + k(ω)). -/
def logPartition (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Real.log (∑ ω : Ω, Real.exp (∑ i, θ i * E.suffStat ω i + E.baseMeasure ω))

/-- Auxiliary: the inner exponent for an exponential family. -/
def expFamilyExponent (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) (ω : Ω) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i, θ i * E.suffStat ω i + E.baseMeasure ω

/-- The pmf of an exponential family. -/
def expFamilyPmf (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) (ω : Ω) : ℝ :=
  Real.exp (expFamilyExponent E θ ω) /
    (∑ ω' : Ω, Real.exp (expFamilyExponent E θ ω'))

omit [DecidableEq Ω] in
theorem expFamilyPmf_nonneg (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) (ω : Ω) :
    0 ≤ expFamilyPmf E θ ω := by
  unfold expFamilyPmf
  positivity

omit [DecidableEq Ω] in
theorem expFamilyPmf_sum_one (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    ∑ ω : Ω, expFamilyPmf E θ ω = 1 := by
  unfold expFamilyPmf
  rw [← Finset.sum_div]
  exact div_self (ne_of_gt (E.partition_pos θ))

/-- Convert an exponential family to a finite statistical model. -/
def ExponentialFamily.toStatModel (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) :
    FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω where
  logLik θ ω := expFamilyExponent E θ ω - logPartition E θ
  pmf := expFamilyPmf E
  pmf_nonneg := expFamilyPmf_nonneg E
  pmf_sum_one := expFamilyPmf_sum_one E
  logLik_spec θ ω _ := by
    unfold expFamilyPmf logPartition expFamilyExponent
    rw [Real.log_div (ne_of_gt (Real.exp_pos _)) (ne_of_gt (E.partition_pos θ)),
        Real.log_exp]

/-- Expectation parameter η(θ) = 𝔼_θ[T] = ∑_ω p(ω;θ) T(ω). -/
def expectationParameter (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    Fin n → ℝ :=
  fun i => ∑ ω : Ω, E.toStatModel.pmf θ ω * E.suffStat ω i

/-- Covariance matrix of the sufficient statistic under the model. -/
def sufficientStatCov (E : ExponentialFamily n Ω) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ :=
  Matrix.of fun i j =>
    (∑ ω : Ω, E.toStatModel.pmf θ ω * E.suffStat ω i * E.suffStat ω j) -
    (∑ ω : Ω, E.toStatModel.pmf θ ω * E.suffStat ω i) *
    (∑ ω : Ω, E.toStatModel.pmf θ ω * E.suffStat ω j)

/-! ## Alpha-connections and Dual Geometry -/

/-- The Amari–Chentsov cubic tensor C_{ijk}(θ) = ∑_ω p(ω;θ) sᵢ(θ,ω) sⱼ(θ,ω) sₖ(θ,ω),
    the third moment of the score. -/
def amariChentsovTensor (M : FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω)
    (dlogp : (Fin n → ℝ) → Ω → Fin n → ℝ) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) :
    Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℝ :=
  fun i j k => ∑ ω : Ω, M.pmf θ ω * dlogp θ ω i * dlogp θ ω j * dlogp θ ω k

/-- The α-Christoffel symbols (lowered, first-kind):
    Γ^(α)_{ij,k} = Γ^(0)_{ij,k} + (α/2) C_{ijk}. -/
def alphaChristoffel (M : FiniteStatModel (Fin n → ℝ) Ω)
    (dlogp : (Fin n → ℝ) → Ω → Fin n → ℝ)
    (leviCivita : (Fin n → ℝ) → Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℝ)
    (α : ℝ) (θ : Fin n → ℝ) : Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℝ :=
  fun i j k => leviCivita θ i j k + (α / 2) * amariChentsovTensor M dlogp θ i j k

/-- The (+1) Christoffel symbols vanish: flatness condition. -/
def PlusOneFlat (Γ : Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j k, Γ i j k = 0

end

# Computational Evidence — Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration

Concise numerical sanity checks supporting the formal theorems in
`Applications/SheafDataIntegration/`. All claims below are *proved* in Lean; this
file only records the small-case evidence that guided the formalization.

## 1. Counting law `#completions = qᵐ`

Setup: value alphabet `α` with `q = #α`; a database over rows `R`; `m =
missingCells D R` is the number of missing cells in the rows of `R`.

`card_dataSection_eq : Fintype.card (DataSection D R) = q ^ m`.

Hand-computed instances (each cell is `Option α`, `•` = observed, `?` = missing):

| database (rows in R) | q | m | predicted `qᵐ` | direct count |
|----------------------|---|---|----------------|--------------|
| `[• •]`              | 2 | 0 | `2^0 = 1`      | 1 (only itself) |
| `[• ?]`              | 2 | 1 | `2^1 = 2`      | 2 (`? ∈ {0,1}`) |
| `[? ?]`              | 2 | 2 | `2^2 = 4`      | 4 |
| `[? ?]`              | 3 | 2 | `3^2 = 9`      | 9 |
| `[• ?; ? •]` (2 rows)| 2 | 2 | `2^2 = 4`      | 4 |

All match. The exponent `m` is a sum over rows (`missingCells` is a `Finset.sum`),
so it is automatically additive over disjoint row blocks — see §3.

## 2. Corollaries cross-checked

* `unique_completion_of_fullyObserved`: `m = 0 ⇒ qᵐ = 1` ✓ (row `[• •]` above).
* `nonunique_completion_of_missing`: `q ≥ 2`, `m ≥ 1 ⇒ qᵐ ≥ 2` ✓ (rows with a `?`).
* `card_dataSection_pos`: `q ≥ 1 ⇒ qᵐ ≥ 1` ✓ (every row above has ≥ 1 completion).

The sequence of completion counts for a single fully-missing row of width `n`
over a binary alphabet is `2^n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …` (OEIS A000079, powers of 2);
over a ternary alphabet `3^n = 1, 3, 9, 27, …` (OEIS A000244). These are exactly
`q ^ (#columns)` when every cell is missing, the `m = n` special case.

## 3. Independence across disjoint row blocks

`card_dataSection_union_disjoint`: for `Disjoint R₁ R₂`,
`#completions(R₁ ∪ R₂) = #completions(R₁) · #completions(R₂)`.

Check: `R₁ = [• ?]` (count 2), `R₂ = [? ?]` (count 4), disjoint rows ⇒ combined
count `2 · 4 = 8 = 2^(1+2)` ✓. The exponents add (`missingCells_union_disjoint`),
the counts multiply — the enumerative shadow of the probabilistic `q ^ C` law.

## 4. Merge / integration

`Database.merge D₁ D₂` keeps observed cells of either source (preferring `D₁`).

* `merge_observed_eq`: observed cells of the merge = union of observed cells ✓
  (`[• ?]` merged with `[? •]` ⇒ `[• •]`, fully observed).
* `consistent_merge_iff` (under agreement on overlaps): completions of the merge
  = assignments consistent with *both* sources. Check on `[• ?]` ⊔ `[? •]` = `[• •]`:
  unique completion, and it is the unique common refinement ✓.
* Monotonicity (`card_dataSection_merge_le_left`): merging `[• ?]` (2 completions)
  with `[? •]` yields `[• •]` (1 completion), and `1 ≤ 2` ✓. Integration never
  increases the completion count, because it can only reveal cells.

## 5. Counterexample hunt

* Forward direction of `consistent_merge_iff` **requires** the agreement
  hypothesis: merging `[• = 0]` with `[• = 1]` on the same cell gives merge `= 0`
  (D₁ preferred); the assignment `0` is consistent with the merge but not with D₂.
  Hence the iff fails without `agree` — the hypothesis is load-bearing, not
  decorative. This is why `agree` appears in the statement.
* No counterexample to the counting law was found across all small cases tried;
  it is now proved in full generality.

# Future Directions — Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration

This cycle established, fully formally (0 sorries, only `propext`,
`Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`):

* **Databases form a sheaf** (`dataSheaf_glue_unique`): compatible local
  completions glue to a *unique* global completion (equalizer/`∃!`).
* **Counting law** (`card_dataSection_eq`): `#completions = q ^ (missing cells)`,
  via an explicit bijection `DataSection ≃ (FreeCell → α)`.
* **Independence across disjoint row blocks** (`card_dataSection_union_disjoint`):
  exponents add, counts multiply.
* **Integration = intersection of section spaces** (`consistent_merge_iff`):
  merging compatible sources intersects their completion spaces; integration is
  monotone (`card_dataSection_merge_le_left`).

The following conjectures are precise and testable targets for the next cycles.

## Conjecture 1 (Inclusion–exclusion for incompatible merges)

When two sources **disagree** on some overlap cells, `consistent_merge_iff`
fails. Conjecture: the number of *jointly* consistent completions is governed by
the agreement locus. Precisely, define `Agree D₁ D₂` = the set of cells where the
sources are both observed and equal. Then the assignments consistent with both
`D₁` and `D₂` are non-empty **iff** the sources agree on every commonly-observed
cell, and in that case their count is `q ^ (cells missing in *both* sources)`.
Testable form: `Nonempty {g // Consistent D₁ R g ∧ Consistent D₂ R g} ↔ (∀ overlap
cells agree)`, and when non-empty its cardinality is `q ^ missingCells (merge) R`.

## Conjecture 2 (Cohomological obstruction to global integration)

Generalize beyond two sources to a cover `{Dₐ}` of partial databases. Conjecture:
a global consistent integration exists **iff** a Čech 1-cocycle assembled from the
pairwise overlap discrepancies is a coboundary, i.e. `H¹ = 0` for the discrepancy
cochain on the overlap nerve. This would connect the `MachineLearning/CechComplex`
machinery (`IsOneCocycle`, `cocycle_eq_coboundary_on_total`) to multi-source
integration, upgrading the pairwise `consistent_merge_iff` to an `n`-source
obstruction theory. Testable: for 3 sources, pairwise compatibility + triangle
cocycle condition ⇒ global section exists.

## Conjecture 3 (Entropy of the completion sheaf)

Under the uniform distribution on completions, the Shannon entropy of the data
sheaf over `R` is exactly `missingCells D R · log q`. Conjecture: entropy is
additive over disjoint row blocks (from `card_dataSection_union_disjoint`) and
*sub*additive under merge: `H(merge D₁ D₂) ≤ min (H D₁) (H D₂)`, with equality iff
the second source observes no new cells. This makes "information gained by
integration" a provable quantity `H(D₁) − H(merge D₁ D₂) = (missing reduction)·log q ≥ 0`.

## Conjecture 4 (Column-wise functional dependencies as a subsheaf)

Restrict the data sheaf to completions satisfying a functional dependency
`X → Y` (rows agreeing on columns `X` must agree on columns `Y`). Conjecture: the
FD-constrained completions form a *subsheaf* (closed under restriction and
gluing), and their count is `q ^ (free cells modulo the FD)` where the exponent
subtracts one degree of freedom per determined cell. Testable: for a single FD on
a 2-row database, the count drops from `q^m` to `q^(m − d)` with `d` the number
of `Y`-cells forced by equal `X`-keys.

## Conjecture 5 (Sheaf of joins / relational algebra)

The natural/inner join of two databases corresponds to a *fibre product* in the
category of data sheaves. Conjecture: `DataSection (join D₁ D₂) ≃` the pullback
`DataSection D₁ ×_{shared} DataSection D₂`, and the counting law specializes to
`#completions(join) = Σ_keys q^(missing in matched rows)`. This would realize the
core relational-algebra operators (select = subsheaf, project = pushforward, join
= pullback) inside the sheaf framework, with `consistent_merge_iff` as the
union/outer-join special case.

concept.title: The Library of Babel: Combinatorics of the Universal Library
concept.concept_description: Borges' Library of Babel contains every possible 410-page book — approximately 25^{1312000} volumes. The library is finite but vast beyond comprehension. Formalize the Library as the set of all strings over a 25-symbol alphabet of length 1312000. Conjecture: The probability that a random volume contains a meaningful proof of a given theorem T is approximately |T| * 25^{-k} where |T| is the length of T and k is the proof complexity of T. Moreover, the Library contains a universal catalog — a single volume that encodes the location of every other volume — and this catalog can be found in polynomial time using a variant of the de Bruijn sequence construction. The deepest question: does the Library contain its own complete catalog? By a diagonal argument, no single volume can encode all volumes (since 25^{1312000} > 1312000 * log_2(25^{1312000})). But a DISTRIBUTED catalog spanning N volumes can encode the entire Library if N > 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_2(25)). Test: compute the exact probability of finding a valid Lean 4 proof of a specific theorem in the Library. Construct a de Bruijn-based catalog for a mini-Library with alphabet size 4 and book length 16. Impact: the mathematics of universal information spaces — every possible text exists, but finding meaning requires a guide.

We generalize the 2×2 block still life from a single example on the 6×6 torus

landscape of stable attractors (still lifes), connecting to description
